utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We will have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Niemann. I appear with my colleague, Mr McHenry, Mr Turone, Mr Dixon and Mr Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Could I have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Zejnil Delalic. With me in the courtroom today, as co-counsels for Mr Delalic, are my colleagues, Mr Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada and Ekrim Galijatovic, attorney, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr Mucic, together with my colleague, Mr Michael Greaves, attorney from the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I am an attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr Hazim Delic along with Mr Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman and Cynthia McMurrey and I appear on behalf of Mr Esad 25 Landzo today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We now have before us the motions and the replies by the Defence. Are you proceeding to argue it this morning? We have oral arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will go first, followed by Mr Moran, and then Ms Residovic and then Mr Olujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHTYE
utterances.text: Before we proceed, I would like to mention what I have observed on the motions. It has been indicated in the motion that it is being argued in the alternative -- that is what your motion says -- and a judgment for acquittal, or alternatively, you proceed to answer the charges against you. Does the Trial Chamber understand that is the alternative in which you are arguing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the alternative is either a judgment of acquittal, or a dismissal of the counts, depending upon whether the decision of the Trial Chamber is based on factual matters demanding acquittal, or legal matters -- jurisdictional matters demanding dismissal. That is the alternative that I think the brief speaks of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is if it is successful?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it is not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it is not successful, of course the Defence goes forward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is where the problem lies. The Rules have always been clear. When you bring motions in that way, you choose either to rest your case on that of the Prosecution evidence and the law, or you decide to merely have a prima facie case and proceed further. If you close your case with that of the evidence for the Prosecution, you would not be entitled to adduce further evidence in rebuttal, because you have now accepted the law and evidence as adduced by the Prosecution and would be bound by it. If, on the other hand, you do not comment on the evidence, and you are challenging the law, and the evidence as not having made a prima facie case, you will be entitled to adduce your own evidence in rebuttal. What I have now seen, your motion has dealt with, in very critical detail, the evidence of the Prosecution and the law, and disputing them in various areas. Now, you are not, strictly speaking, accepting the evidence of the Prosecution -- you are challenging them and asking for a judgment of acquittal, which means you are relying, for your case -- if you are asking for a judgment of acquittal, you are relying for your case on the evidence of the Prosecution -- a case for acquittal, for that you are relying on the case made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No defendant at this stage is resting their case, your Honour. With regard to factual matters, based upon the Tadic Trial Chamber pronouncement of what the burden is at this stage, it is our belief that, at this stage, from a factual matter with regard to each element of each offence, the Prosecution must have established a prima facie case. We are arguing that, with regard to some of the counts, the Prosecution has failed to establish a prima facie case at this point, not that all of the evidence is in and the test should be a "beyond a reasonable doubt" test, but that the Prosecution evidence now is closed and, being what it is, in some instances, we believe that the Prosecution has failed to establish a prima facie case, that is, bring forward some evidence as to each element of each offence and that is the argument that we are making. It is not an argument that the evidence is closed and that you should weigh the evidence to make a determination as to whether there is proof beyond a reasonable doubt or not. That is not our contention, that is not what we are asking the Trial Chamber to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Then your choice lies on the aspect which still expected that there are disputed facts, in which case you still come forward to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No question about it -- if they have made a prima facie case as to each element, then we will go forward and contest that. If they have not, then this court should dismiss those particular counts of the indictment where they have not made the prima facie case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When you put it in the alternative, you have to make a choice as to which alternative you take, but you do not have your cake and eat it -- it must be one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may very well be that titling the motion, a motion for judgment of acquittal and motion to dismiss, was not all that artful, having no reason to believe that the court would view the language "acquittal" as being somehow a contention that it is time to weigh the evidence and make a decision based upon the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. All we are suggesting is, if there is factual insufficiency, such that there is no prima facie evidence with regard to a particular element of a particular count, then either an acquittal or a dismissal would lie -- not knowing which of those might be the appropriate remedy, we chose to state it in the alternative so, if the court felt that acquittal was appropriate, because of the lack of a prima facie case, the court would be able to do that. If that was in error, then we certainly would withdraw any argument of acquittal and simply say that count should be dismissed because of a lack of a prima facie case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do appreciate that in every motion for dismissal based on the fact that no prima facie case has been made, it affects only those areas where such prima facie case has not been made. For areas where they have been made, they go forward to defend that. If it has not been made, it must be dismissed -- the usual situation. When you talk about acquittal resting on determination of the facts and the like, you are assuming that you are resting your case on that of the Prosecution, which normally should not be -- the result could have been the same, whichever way you choose, but depending on your own choice -- because if you feel so convinced, if you feel so strongly that you do not have to go forward to give evidence, that sort of rests on the case of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can only speak on behalf of Mr Landzo on that issue, but I assure you that Mr Landzo does not rest his case at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I will take the blame for the phrase "judgment of acquittal". The practice I am used to is, at the close of the Prosecutor's case, if they have failed to make a prima facie case, a judgment of acquittal is actually entered rather than dismissal and so I will take the blame for that inartful wording and apologise to the court if I confused you -- or if I confused myself. But, on behalf of Mr Delic, if the court finds that there is a prima facie case made on any of the counts on which he is charged, we will present evidence. All we are asking the court to do is to view the evidence in the light most favourable to the Prosecutor and determine whether they have made a prima facie case as to each count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the legal system that I come from, at this stage of the proceedings, a decision is taken on suspending the proceedings on the basis of a ruling of the court whether there is still reasonable grounds to suspect that the accused has committed a criminal offence. In the wording of our motion, we relied on the experiences of our colleagues from the common law system and that is why the motion was worded alternatively. We claim that there is no prima facie case and if that implies dismissing the indictment, we abide by that, but if the Trial Chamber finds that a prima facie case has been established for any element of the counts against him, the Defence will present its evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to Mr Zdravko Mucic, I should like to underline that we also believe that, at the end of the examination-in-chief, a motion can be made to dismiss the indictment, and that is what we have tried to argue in our written brief from which it is visible that our proposal is directed in that direction in the first place, that is, that no prima facie case has been established, but if the court should not accept such a position, then the Defence will continue with presenting its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We now know where we are -- there was confusion as to the procedure being adopted. You have all read each other's submissions, so I think the areas of real disagreement might be -- I have not read this one (indicating), which has just been received this morning, but I have read the other submissions and if you can only now possibly limit yourself to those areas which you think you want to emphasise, instead of going through the whole system. We have the documents themselves, so let us hear argument on the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want again to say good morning to your Honours and to my colleagues of the Prosecution. As you have suggested, your Honours, I intend to be quite brief. I believe that the briefs that have been filed in this matter are extraordinarily comprehensive; that the issues have been very clearly written and set out before you; and there is not a great deal more that can be said that is not confined within the pages of the briefs. I think they have been fairly written, fairly argued and fairly presented to you. It may be that you have questions about some matters that are contained in the brief that, between the four of us, we will be able to respond to, to the extent we can. The defendants Landzo, Delic and Delalic, in addition to presenting to you a joint brief, will also present to you a joint argument so that each of us will not seek to address each of the matters raised in the briefs, but divide it up and each of us will address some different portion of that which we have argued to you in writing. I will talk to you, very briefly, about the issues of international armed conflict and whether or not common Article 3 is incorporated within Article 3 so as to give this court jurisdiction over common Article 3 (charged offences). To begin, I think it is important to set the stage, so to speak. This Tribunal was created pursuant to Chapter 7 of the Charter of the United Nations for the purpose of assisting the United Nations in restoring peace and security to the former Yugoslavia. So, the primary mission then of this Tribunal is to do what it can to assist in that process. The specific mission based upon that is, of course, to bring to trial, in a fair and meaningful way, those persons accused of having committed violations of international humanitarian law during the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. Clearly, when you view the mission as being one of assisting the United Nations in restoring peace and security to the former Yugoslavia, that necessarily implies that this court's mission is a public one. It is one that cannot succeed but for the perception that the residents of former Yugoslavia and the rest of the world have of this court. The rest of the world and the residents of the former Yugoslavia must be able to view this court as a calming influence, as a place where justice is the watchword, as a place where fairness is the watchword. I think this court can never hope, in its most ambitious expectations, to satisfy certain radical elements in Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, that it is a just court. I think that is a false hope, because, when Serbians are on trial, Serbs will always see you as being unfair for putting them on trial in the first place. We have seen that in the press, we have seen that in letters that have been sent to the Office of the Prosecutor from various organisations. We see criticism from the radicals of what we are doing here, so we cannot hope to influence, I think, those people, but we can hope to influence and to show both the world and the residents of former Yugoslavia that this is a place that is fair, that this is a place that is just, and it is a place in which they can put their confidence. That is what I would hope as we look back on the work of this court, years from now, to be able to conclude that this Tribunal did. The key then, to me, to accomplishing that, is an abiding concern for law and justice and, to accomplish law and justice, I think the most important thing in any society is that we have an independent judiciary; judges who can be counted on to apply the law as it has been given to them, with honesty, with dignity, and without fear or favour. If we look back in history at the judges we all remember from history, the ones we have learned about in our studies, the ones we have read about in our readings who are revered, without exception, those are judges who, both at the time they sat on the bench and at the time -- and today, are seen as having been just and have operated with that honesty and integrity and without fear or favour. Many, many times what they did on a particular day was not popular. What they did on a particular day was not acceptable to many people, but, looking back, we know that they were just, we know that they were fair and that is why we revere them. They demonstrated in their work an independence which is the watchword for a judge, and they demonstrated a commitment to law and justice, which we all now very much appreciate. All we can ask of you, and all the parties I think in this room ask of you, is to be that kind of judge. It is important that, at the end of the day, this Tribunal be seen as having been a just place in which law was paramount. Let me address very briefly the issue of international armed conflict. Your Honours know full well that the Tadic Trial Chamber addressed that issue in its decision in the Tadic case, and made findings essentially that there was no international armed conflict after 19 May 1992, and concluded that, as a result of that, the persons were not protected because it was not international armed conflict. The question that we have raised and one that is of issue before you is what is the effect on this Trial Chamber of that decision by the Tadic Trial Chamber. We argue to you, and have argued to you, that it should have a binding effect, or at least a strong persuasive effect for this reason: the Office of the Prosecutor was a party to that case. The issues regarding international armed conflict in that case were identical to those in this case. The Office of the Prosecutor had a full, fair and complete opportunity to present evidence and to argue and brief that evidence before that Tadic Trial Chamber -- and they did so. Unless the Office of the Prosecutor has brought before this Trial Chamber evidence that was not available to it at the time of the Tadic trial, evidence that did not exist at the time of the Tadic trial, then it is our contention that, under the doctrine of collateral estoppel, they should not be permitted to re-raise the factual aspects of that Tadic decision, but only the legal issues that might be involved with it, because, they should be estopped from continually attempting to establish the same thing in the same way, since they were a party to that prior case. The question, if that is correct, then becomes: what is there in the Celebici trial that differs from what was presented by the Office of the Prosecutor in the Tadic trial? Our suggestion to you is that there is no difference that is meaningful. The primary testimony in the Tadic trial was that of Dr Gow -- the primary testimony in this trial on that issue is that of Dr Gow. You will recall that Dr Gow sat in that witness chair and was asked, "What new information about international armed conflict did you bring to us today that you did not know when you testified in the Tadic trial?" His response was, "There is no new information. There may be some things that I have learned since Tadic, but they do not change my broad standing of what occurred in the former Yugoslavia". The Office of the Prosecutor has suggested to you that the diary of Borisav Jovic, which was admitted as an exhibit in the Celebici case, was not available at the time of the Tadic trial and that that is a difference. However, in the Tadic trial, as you will recall Dr Gow telling you, the segment of a videotape from the BBC programme on, "The Death of Yugoslavia", in which Borisav Jovic, he said the same things as he said in the diary, so the Tadic Trial Chamber had exactly the same information before it. I think more important than that, it is not whether or not new evidence came to you that was not available to Tadic but what the quality of that evidence is. It can only have impact if that evidence were specifically directed to the issue of effective control by FRY over Bosnian Serb forces. That was the issue that was paramount before the Tadic Trial Chamber and that is the issue that is paramount here. There can be no international armed conflict if FRY was not exerting effective control over the activities of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can a finding on the question of a fact be relevant in another case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under the doctrine of collateral estoppel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Without a finding of fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Between the same parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As long as there is a party identity, and, in this case, there is a party identity; the Office of the Prosecutor was a party in both cases. What we suggesting is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure that that is how you look at it. Each case has its own evidence, it has to be viewed independently. Can a finding of fact given in another case be regarded as relevant in another case, just like a finding in a criminal case is not relevant in a civil case even if the parties are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It can be, I think, and it really depends. When a fact has been found against a party, as it has been found against the Office of the Prosecutor in the Tadic case, then, because they were a party in the Tadic case and also a party in this case, it is my argument that they cannot continue as a party in successive cases to assert the same factual basis and seek a different result. Whether or not it is binding on this Tribunal of course is going to be up to this Trial Chamber. That is a decision you have to make, but it seems to me that, even if you will not go so far as to say you are bound by it, you certainly must give a great deal of weight to the view of your fellow judges, who, I know, very carefully listened to and considered that issue in Tadic. So, it may only be persuasive, and that is still okay with me -- it should be persuasive to you. Have I answered your question, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As best as you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I have covered basically what I wanted to say about international armed conflict. We contend, of course, that that is an element of every count of the indictment, because the indictment incorporates that paragraph into every count by its specific language, so that, with regard to each count of the indictment, one of the things the Office of the Prosecutor must prove is international armed conflict. Let me now speak again, I hope briefly, about Article 3 of Statute and whether or not common Article 3 is incorporated therein. I invite you to look carefully at what we have written with regard to that. I do not want to expound on that to any particular degree. One of the questions that is raised before you is the extent to which you might be bound by the decision of the Tadic Appellate Chamber regarding whether or not common Article 3 is within the jurisdiction of this court. We suggest that you should not, and we suggest you should not for a number of reasons. First of all, we must have firmly in mind when we consider that that that Tadic Appellate Chamber decision was a preliminary decision based upon motions that had been filed in the case -- not a decision following a complete trial of the case, and a complete argument and briefing of all of the issues. It can be seen as perhaps nothing more than a permission for the case to go forward, putting the Prosecutor to their burden to prove that common Article 3 is part of customary international law, and we believe both in the Tadic trial and in the Celebici trial, the Prosecutor has utterly and completely failed in that burden. The reason we say in addition that the Tadic appellate decision is not binding upon you is that whether or not something is a part of customary international law is a mixed question of law and fact. It is not just a legal issue, because, as you know, a party who contends that some body of law has become part of customary international law, according to the ICJ, has the burden of giving a factual background to support that. What is the practice of States with regard to this issue? Do States generally consider this body of law to be applicable to them? Do the writers in the field fairly uniformly consider this body of law to be customary international law? Those are the kind of things you must always enquire into when determining whether something is customary international law or not. The opinio juris it is called with regard to opinions of courts around the world and the opinion of justices around the world. When you view common Article 3 in that context, I think it fails. It is quite clear, I believe, that that Appellate Tribunal did not have before it everything that it should have had before it to make such a far-reaching decision, and that can be the result of a number of things, one of them being that it was a preliminary motion not adequately briefed and not adequately argued. The Office of the Prosecutor has taken the position, for instance, in its response to the pre-trial briefs of the defendants in this case, that, with regard to an issue that had been decided by the Tadic Appellate Chamber, that it had not been fully briefed and argued and, therefore, should not be binding on you, so to some extent we both agree on whether or not something has been adequately briefed and argued should have something to do with whether it has binding effect or not. There is nothing, for instance, in the Tadic appellate decision that refers to the statement -- the report of the Secretary-General of the United Nations on the establishment of the Rwanda Tribunal, that is not mentioned in the Tadic appellate decision, apparently was not considered, or perhaps not even known to the judges who arrived at that decision, and I think it is a compelling and telling statement by the Secretary-General when he says with regard to the Rwanda Statute that in that Statute common Article 3 is being criminalised for the first time, almost two years after the adoption of the Statute of this court and the Office of the Prosecutor has not responded to our argument in that regard, they have not tried to explain to this Tribunal why it is the Secretary-General would have said that, if he did not believe it to be true and if it were not the law, or why the Security Council, in adopting a Statute for the Rwanda Tribunal, specifically included an article specifically incorporating common Article 3. If the Security Council had believed at the time of the Rwanda Statute in its adoption that common Article 3 was included in the ICTY Statute, then there would be no reason to do anything but put Article 3 of the ICTY Statute in its entirety into the Rwanda Statute. There is a reason why a specific section was written incorporating common Article 3. It was because it was the first time they were interested in doing that and the Secretary-General said, for the first time common Article 3 is being criminalised, several years after all of the events that are before you in this case occurred -- four years after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just want to find out factual information. Was Rwanda a party to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. I think so. I think there were only a couple of States in the world, two or three, Burma I know is one, who is not a party. So I think Rwanda probably was, and I can supplement, if you would like me to, by letter, and advise you of that within the next 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like me to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I would like to know for my information only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will find out tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It has not bearing at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Alright. The final thing I want to discuss with you on this issue is the response by the Office of the Prosecutor that, by looking at the statements of various representatives to the Security Council at the time of the adoption of the ICTY Statute, it is clear that there was an intention that common Article 3 be included as under 3 of the ICTY Statute. A close and fair reading, your Honours, of those remarks, I think makes it abundantly clear that that is not the case; that those representatives were not suggesting in their remarks that common Article 3 was part of the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. I would like to specifically refer to that. The brief response of the Office of the Prosecutor on that issue mentioned the remarks of the French delegate, the US delegate, the delegate from the United Kingdom and the delegate from Hungary. The French delegate, in speaking about Article 3 of the Statute, said this: "I should like to make a few brief comments on this subject" -- that being the Statute -- "firstly, the expression 'laws or customs of war' used in Article 3 of the Statute covers specifically, in the opinion of France, all the obligations that flow from the humanitarian law agreements in force on the territory of the former Yugoslavia." He is talking about the agreement of 22 May that was entered into between Republika Srbska, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding the application of portions of the Geneva Convention under the auspices of the International Committee of the Red Cross. If you go to Ms Albright's remarks, you see the same thing. She says: "Firstly, it is understood that the laws and customs of war referred to in Article 3 include all obligations under humanitarian law agreements in force in the territory of the former Yugoslavia at the time the acts were committed, including common Article 3 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, and the 1977 Additional Protocols to these Conventions." Her understanding that that agreement of 22 May included common Article 3 and Protocol 1. If you look at the remarks of Sir David Hannay from the UK, he just very peripherally mentions Article 3 of the Statute and says nothing about common Article 3, or any humanitarian law agreements and if you look at the comments of Mr Erdos from Hungary he speaks about neither common Article 3 or Article 3. I have noted in my brief and will just very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This 22 May agreement, I think the last clause states it will come into force after the parties have ratified it; did the parties ratify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. They may have, but not to my knowledge. That is another issue upon which I think the Office of the Prosecutor and us are in agreement, that that agreement of 22 May has no impact on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because it was not alleged in the indictment and no part of the indictment is based on the contents of that agreement. The Tadic Appellate Tribunal has spoken to that, the Office of the Prosecutor has conceded that and we have of course argued that, but it is interesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: After you have finished with this, the declaration of war issued, I think some time in June, by the Bosnian State -- there is a clause 4 there with regard to the application of humanitarian laws and conventions. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not have a specific recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Declaration of war - it is one of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think, just kind of in closing, that it is real clear when you look at the statements of these representatives, that they were not talking in the context of their understanding that common Article 3 was incorporated into Article 3, but only their understanding that it might be possible to charge common Article 3 offences under Article 3, based upon the agreement of 22 May that had been entered into by the warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Three parties are mentioned who have committed aggression. One is the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro; secondly, JNA; and, thirdly, the Terrorist Democratic Party, whatever it is -- I am talking about the proclamation of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That general issue, I specifically discussed with Dr Gow. It is one of the problems -- I think one of the major problems that this Trial Chamber and all Trial Chambers in this court have to deal with, and will always have to deal with. That is the issue of credibility. The issue of credibility is so much more pronounced here than in any international court that I have ever appeared in. The difference is profound, because the pronouncements of parties to the conflict in Yugoslavia were frequently pronouncements in an effort to achieve a certain result, but without regard to whether or not it was really true. You will recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. You can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You will, for instance, recall when I was talking with Dr Gow about Lord Owen, and his comments about the most perplexing and frustrating part of his work was trying to find out what was the truth, that he had a very difficult time getting people to tell him the truth. One thing that is extraordinarily clear was that, for a significant period of time, the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was very anxious for the world to see them as victims of external aggression to try to get aid to assist them in their efforts. I think we cannot look to a statement like that that has a clear political purpose, but, rather, look at what we know about what was going on on the ground and what we can learn about what was going on on the ground, so I think, perhaps that is an answer to your question, Judge Jan. I think I have concluded the remarks that I wanted to make to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me see whether you can clarify a few things. Your argument with respect to Article 3, the common Article 3 being part of Article 3 of the Statute, has been based on the interpretation of the words of Article 3 of the Statutes. You tried to suggest that the items indicated in Article 3 did not envisage those which were the type of warfare materials envisaged in common Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But do you think that is consistent with the definition of the words "shall include", which is expansive in nature, and not necessarily exclusive of other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there clearly in Article 3 is a clause which permits incorporation of other offences within Article 3. There is no question about that. One way I have talked about this to my colleagues is if a State were to pass a penal statute which says, "The following things among others shall be illegal -- breaking open parking meters, spitting on the sidewalk, throwing rocks through windows" and then a Prosecutor were to say, "Well, since it is said 'among other things', we are going to charge murder under this statute," we would all see that as totally preposterous and ridiculous because the principle of crimen sine lege says you are entitled to know what a statute prohibits and any time you have language in a statute which says, "the following things among others shall be illegal", you have serious problems with that principle. The only way in my view that you can conform that statute to that principle is if the "among others" only refers to like offences -- similar offences. Clearly, Article 3, if you compare it to The Hague Convention, was simply an attempt by the writer to place in statutory form the provisions of The Hague Convention. No effort was made there, and clearly no effort was made there, to incorporate common Article 3. When the Security Council wanted to put common Article 3 in a Statute for an International Tribunal, they did it. They did it directly, they did it completely, they did it in a full article of the ICTR Statute. You have to look not only at the meaning of those words "among others" and what could be included there, but you have to look at the intent of the Security Council. It seems to me that intent is extremely clear when you look at what happened with the ICTR Statute, and when you look at the remarks of the Secretary-General regarding that Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not speaking here about the subsequent experience. The Rwanda Statute is a subsequent experience, which perhaps might have occurred to them to specifically do after the experience of the ICTY. Although one would say that when the ICTY was drafted, one could have construed the provision to include all other matters which could be read meaningfully to it. I am not saying that that was the intention -- I did not say so. I am merely saying that if it was subsequently specifically so named does not mean that that could not be read into it, if the offences, or the like offences could be associated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If, your Honour, that is the case, if that can be read broadly enough to include something entirely different from the list, then that is only part of the exercise. The next part of the exercise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not analogous at all. To "include" does not merely mean inter alia. "Inclusion" incorporates many more things than that. This is not a case where perhaps you are referring to it generally. They are talking about violations of law and the concepts of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is contained in there is what is generally referred to by writers as, "the law of The Hague", which deals with the matter in the way the war is conducted, not humanitarian issues. In addition, and I think this is crucial, when the Office of the Prosecutor seeks to incorporate into Article 3 something contended to be customary international law, as the ICJ says, they have the burden of proving that. They have the burden of proving, because they have alleged common Article 3 in this case, that common Article 3 is part of customary international law. I submit that is a burden which simply cannot be met. You would think that if one could even come close to achieving that burden, you would at least be able to show one case from anywhere in the world where common Article 3 was the basis for a criminal Prosecution. Now, I am sure you, Judge Karibi-Whyte, know a great deal more about this than any of us in the rest of the room do, but the Tadic Appellate Chamber referred to a couple of prosecutions from your country, Nigeria, and their reference appears to be newspaper articles and they concluded, apparently, that those prosecutions may have been based on common Article 3. I think they probably were not. Another of the Nigerian cases they refer to in that regard we have managed to get our hands on, and it was based strictly on domestic murder law and the trial was on domestic murder law. It was a situation where a Biafran officer killed a Biafran soldier and in that case the murder prosecution was based strictly on domestic murder law -- nothing in there about common Article 3. I hunch that is the same with the other two cases, but you are probably in a better position to know that than any of us and I would certainly defer to your knowledge of your own country in that regard. But nowhere else have any of us been able to find one case where common Article 3 formed the basis for a criminal prosecution. It cannot be part of the opinio juris of the nations if nobody treats it that way. The United States Congress, after the remarks of Ms Albright before the Security Council, adopted the War Crimes Act of 1996, criminalising the grave breaches provisions of the Geneva Convention of 1949, but specifically refusing to include therein common Article 3 violations, so as late as 1996 the United States Congress did not believe it was customary international law and part of the opinio juris and did not include it in the Statute. May I answer any other questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see your point. I see you are relying on the comment that the Rwanda trial was the first time common Article 3 has been criminalised by legislation. The criminalisation of humanitarian infractions have not been so common. It is not known to be so regularly done, except perhaps a country decides to do it on its own. Even if it is that new, it would not surprise anyone. It may be one of the slips of legislation. This does not really represent my view. I am only listening to arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If that is true, if what the Secretary-General said is true, that it was criminalised for the first time by that Statute, and there is no evidence that anybody challenged that statement, the Security Council adopted that report, there is no evidence that any member of the Security Council said, "Wait a minute, we did that with the ICTY Tribunal". It was an accepted statement. If it is true that it was criminalised at that time for the first time, then it was not in 1992, when the events that are the subject of this case occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Ackerman, but that may be an argument at that time and parallels can be drawn later, even outside the floor of such arguments, reminding other persons of the same pattern (INAUDIBLE) legislations. Because nobody mentioned it there does not mean that it could have been done (INAUDIBLE) legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: However, it is in our view the burden of the Office of the Prosecutor, when they suggest that common Article 3 is part of customary international law to show that to you and to prove that to you under the very, very strict requirements that have been adopted on a number of occasions by the ICJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just very briefly add a personal note. This may very well be the last time that I will stand and address you. I want to tell you how much I have enjoyed being here, how privileged I felt being here, how much I have enjoyed the repartee and relationship I have had with this court and all my other colleagues in this Trial Chamber. I will miss you all very much, and I care a great deal about all of you, and I will be a bit lonely for a while back in Houston, Texas. I hope maybe some day I can come back and see you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have enjoyed all your contributions. We hope we will have another opportunity to meet you at some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court, good morning, your Honours. I would like to talk about a couple of things. I am going to keep it short. The first thing I would like to chat about is the Prosecution's argument that this court should not be determining what the elements of the offence are at this stage. Secondly, I would like to talk about the nationality issue that has come up. Thirdly, I would talk a little bit about the status of people as prisoners of war. Then I will talk in general about command responsibility and apply that to the Delic case in particular, because it stands in a little bit different posture. In their response to our memorandum, the Prosecutor says on page 9 of his brief -- 9 and 10 -- basically, that this is not an appropriate time for the Trial Chamber to be citing what the elements of the offence are and we ought to wait until all the evidence is in, and you hear the arguments of counsel before you decide what constitutes a crime. To me, that is a rather foreign concept. I thought that crimes were defined and then there was an indictment for a crime, and then the Prosecution was put to its burden of proving each of the elements of that offence and then, at this stage of the trial, if there was a contention that the Prosecutor had failed to make a prima facie case as to one or more of the elements of one of the counts, the court had to decide, and I do not know how this court can conceivably rule on this motion unless it has a feel and decides what constitutes a crime. The Prosecutor's position that they laid out in their indictment what they think is a crime, and that is what they have to prove is a rather foreign concept. When the Security Council created this court, the Security Council did not pass a law, it did not create new crimes, it did not create new definitions of crimes, because the Security Council is not a legislative body. What the Security Council did was set up a Tribunal to consider and hear allegations that certain people violated certain laws. The Statute itself, while you look at it and we talk about the Statute as creating this crime and that crime, in fact what the Statute does is simply give this court the power to hear certain kinds of things. I do not think that anyone would argue that -- I am sure that the Secretary-General would not -- the Statute created a law or created a crime, or defined a crime, because in his report the Secretary-General, in paragraph 34, was very clear that all they were trying to do was create a Tribunal to consider those allegations, and I think this will become a little crucial as we go a little further into my argument. There are some areas where it appears that the Statute of the Tribunal may have defined offences slightly differently, or somewhat differently, or even greatly differently, than the relevant conventions, which we may be here to interpret and apply. With that, I will go to the issue of nationality. The court is real familiar with our position -- I have made it clear since my initial pre-trial brief that was filed, I hate to say this, over a year ago, and our position is to be a protected person under the Geneva Convention on Civilians, what I refer to as the GCC, one has to meet the definition in -- in article 4 of that Convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting in your first argument that there should be definitions of substantive offences in international criminal law from which the Prosecution could have derived its criminality of offences?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I am saying is this, your Honour: what I am saying is that there is international law that is out there, this international law was out there prior to the date this Tribunal was created, and this international law will be out there prior to the date that this Tribunal ceases -- excuse me, subsequent to the date that this Tribunal ceases to exist. The law may change, laws are always a growing and changing concept. What I am suggesting, your Honour, is this: when the Security Council created this Tribunal, the Security Council lacked the authority to pass laws. I think everyone is agreed on that. If you read my initial brief, I cite a man, I believe, named Douglas, who wrote a Law Review article, taking that position -- I think it is a proper position -- that what the Security Council was doing was, instead of creating offences or defining offences, it was creating a forum for trials and, yes, your Honour, there is some law out there -- there has to be, or you cannot have a crime. Some of it is customary law of war, and some of it is conventional law of war. For instance, I think everyone has taken the position that the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 constitute substantive law. They are not designed and they were not written to be penal statutes but they are substantive international law. The additional Protocols of 1977, I think, constitute substantive law, and you can look at those Protocols, and you can decide, and you can determine what is the law and then apply that law. I think it becomes more difficult, frankly, when you are talking about customary law of war, because in customary law of war, we do not have somebody, some conference meeting in wherever the conference met in 1949, to hash out a written document, and we have to look at how these laws have been applied and in customary law we also have to look, I think, to what the nations of the world think international law is, so that the nations of the world will say, "This is customary international law, because everybody applies it this way and we believe we are required to apply it". The best example I will be talking about in a minute is command responsibility. We have both customary and conventional law there. The customary law is really built around five or six cases that were tried after World War II, the Yamashita case, the hostages case, the high command case, the Toyoda case and, to some extent, the Tokyo Tribunal and based on that, the nations of the world have said, "Command responsibility is this"; and they have begun to apply it. Both sides have cited to you, for instance, on the issue of command responsibility, the appropriate military manuals from the United States and Great Britain. We have also cited to you the decree from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its military regulations. When you look at those, that shows how the nations of the world interpret customary law of war. As I say, your Honour, it is probably more difficult to interpret customary law than it would be to interpret conventional law, because you have something that is a document that you can look at, but it is there. The World Court, the ICJ, has always recognised customary law, international law. They apply it every day. It is part of the body of law. Have I answered your question, I hope, or have I gone too far in answering it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. On the issue of nationality, this is something that is an Article 2 count. It is clearly governed by the -- whether these people are protected persons is clearly governed by article 4 of the Geneva Convention on Civilians. It says, "These people are protected." It uses the phrase, I believe, "in the hands of a party of which he is not a national". If you are not in the hands of a party of which you are not a national you are not a protected person under article 4 of the Geneva Convention on Civilians. We think the word "nationality" has a pretty common and accepted meaning among international lawyers, and we think that this Trial Chamber -- any court -- anyone in the world is quite capable of reading that paragraph in the Geneva Conventions. It is not ambiguous, it is not unclear. The Prosecutor seems to think that it is, or that it should not be applied for various reasons, that we should not give these words their common accepted meaning. My position is that we should. I think that the only evidence we have had on what constitutes a nationality came from Professor Economides. He was here to help us with what constitutes both conventional and customary international law. Right now, there is not a lot of conventional international law on nationalities. Professor Economides and his colleagues on the ILC are trying to write some, but I think it was his testimony as to what is customary law and what is the practice of nations right now, because nations believe that that is the law, is that, upon a secession or disintegration of a country, people become nationals of the area where they are habitually a resident, or, stated a little differently and maybe a bit better, if a person is a habitual resident of an area and that area becomes a separate State, they become nationals of that country. At some point they may have an option of choice to choose a different nationality, but that is something that they have to exercise. There is absolutely no evidence in this case that anyone ever attempted to exercise any kind of choice. There is absolutely no evidence in this case, in fact, that the residents of the Konjic area, who became citizens or nationals of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, upon the independence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact ever had a real right of option, that they could have chosen a different nationality other than Bosnia. In fact, one of the exhibits that I introduced through Professor Gow was the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There are two articles in there, article 2 and I believe article 17, which, when read together, make it clear as there can be that there was no right of option under that constitution. There is -- I am not sure whether this is a factual question or not before the court. I have been thinking about this all night. Professor Economides testified as to the demise of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said that it ceased to exist on the day the Security Council passed a resolution and I asked him whether the Security Council recognised what had already happened, or whether by this resolution it ceased to exist. He insisted it ceased to exist on the day the Security Council passed the resolution. Dr Gow took a slightly different position. He said the State ceased to exist when the person representing the President was not allowed to become the President. That is Dr Gow's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes. My position is the secession of the SFRY is more a legal question. I do not think there is a credibility choice between Dr Economides -- whether he is telling the truth or Professor Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is not a question of truth but a question of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is right. I think this Trial Chamber can decide, has the evidence before it to decide as a matter of law the SFRY ceased to exist on a certain date. Even if that date was after May of 1992, based on Professor Economides' explanation of nationality, the residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina may very well have been dual nationals of SFRY and Bosnia-Herzegovina, but, when the Socialist Federal Republic ceased to exists, and I believe that was on 27 April at the latest, but that is something for the court to decide, there was no more SFRY, there was no more SFRY nationality and everybody became a national of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, at that point, until there was some affirmative effort to break that nationality bond or to accept another nationality, everybody there, regardless of their status as inmates, prisoners, guards, members of the Bosnian military, or members of the Bosnian Government, they all remained nationals of Bosnia Herzegovina until such time as, in Professor Economides' testimony, they made an affirmative act to break that -- to accept another nationality. Your Honour, I just notice there is a break due in five minutes. Can I finish this section and then break and come back, or do you want me to -- I may be a little more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will rise and come back at 12 o'clock. The Trial Chamber will rise and resume at 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, why have I talked so much about nationality? The reason for that is this is an Article 2 count. The Prosecutor bears the burden of bringing evidence to show that these are protected people. The Prosecutor is trying to make the issue whether or not they are identified with one side or the other; whether or not the fact that someone can be protected under the Geneva Convention on Prisoners of War without regard to his nationality has some bearing on how one would apply the Geneva Convention on Civilians. Your Honours, I just think that that -- all that is totally irrelevant. If the drafters of the Conventions would have wanted to say that people are protected if they are identified with one side or another, they knew how to say that. They made it very, very clear -- Pictet's commentaries which we cited and quoted at some length are perfectly clear as to what they said and what they meant. Furthermore, both the Tadic Appellate Chamber and the Tadic Trial Chamber seems to have rejected the Prosecutor's argument. In paragraph 76, I believe it is, of the Tadic appellate opinion Judge Cassese set out a hypothetical situation where Bosnian Serbs were in the hands of Bosnian Muslims and the Appeals Chamber said, clearly, Bosnian Serbs did not constitute a State, they would not be in the hands of a party to which they are not a national. It just turns out that that hypothetical, which was handed down about four months before the indictment in this case, is the facts of this case. In the Tadic Trial Chamber decision from last May, if you look at both the majority opinion and Judge McDonald's dissenting opinion, there was no question about the nationality -- it did not turn on that, the question of whether or not the Bosnian Muslims who were in the hands of Tadic and his cohorts were in the hands of a party to a conflict of which they were not nationals. The Trial Chamber basically said that the Bosnian Serbs -- the Bosnian Serb forces were not the agents of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; therefore, they were not protected persons. That is clearly an implicit finding, that the Bosnian Serbs, and the Bosnian Muslims share the same nationality, so both the Tadic Appellate and Tadic Trial Chamber seem to agree with our position. Jumping ahead to the issue of prisoners of war, if the people who were inmates in the Celebici prison are to be protected under international law -- article 2 under the Conventions, they have to be either civilians or prisoners of war. In our initial submission, we did not discuss prisoners of war, except to say that there is no evidence that they are. The Prosecution in its response said, "Well, some of them may have been prisoners of war, and besides you can decide they were either prisoners of war or civilians who were protected by the Geneva Convention on Civilians." The first thing I would suggest is that the Prosecutor has to show, as part of the case on article 2, that they were protected persons. You cannot say, "well, maybe they were this", or, "maybe they were that". They have to prove each one of their named complaining witnesses is. Is this person a civilian or is this person a prisoner of war. As to prisoners of war, I laid out in our response the article 4 definition. It is at page 19 in our response that was filed yesterday. The Geneva Convention on Prisoners of War lists six kinds of people who can have prisoner of war status, and in a short version, one of them is members of the armed forces of a party to the conflict -- that can be militia or volunteer corps, as long as they are part of the armed forces. The second thing is members of militias or other volunteer corps, including organised resistance units belonging to a party to the conflict, and those groups have to meet four conditions. They have to be commanded by a person responsible for subordinates, they have to have a fixed distinctive sign recognisable at a distance, they have to carry their arms openly and they have to conduct their operations in accordance with the laws and customs of war. The third possibility is members of regular armed forces possessing an allegiance to a Government or authority not recognised by the detaining power. That is the Free French from World War II. Pictet is clear that that was put in to regularise the status of the Free French. The fourth group is persons who accompany the armed forces -- that is air crews, war correspondents, that type of thing. The fifth group is members of -- crews of ships. The sixth group is the levee en masse, the people who rise up spontaneously on the approach of an invader, to defend their homes. They, too, must meet two criteria -- that of carrying arms openly and respectimg the laws and customs of war. It is our submission that the only two possibilities it could be here is -- to make the inmates in the Celebici prisoners of war -- is that they are either members of resistance groups, or a levee en masse. Let me show you why the evidence is clear from the Prosecution's witnesses, taken in the light most favourable to the Prosecutor, why they are not entitled to prisoner of war status. Uniformly, they denied that they were wearing uniforms, with one exception and I will get that to that one in a moment. They denied they were wearing uniforms or fixed signs. There was no testimony at all that they were commanded by a commander who was responsible for his subordinates. The Prosecutor has failed to show that they conducted their operations in accordance with the laws and customs of war. But in a more basic thing, the Prosecutor alleges in his response that these people were part of the Serb military. I did not hear any evidence of that. Maybe I missed something, maybe I was not here one day, but I did not hear anybody say, "We are part of the Bosnian Serb military". It was just the opposite -- the testimony from person after person after person was that; "We organised ourselves to defend our homes." With one exception, which I believe was Witness M. The Prosecutor cites in their response several pages of testimony, transcript testimony, showing where these people had testified -- various witnesses testified in such a way that it may give them prisoner of war status. We decided to go in and just give you that testimony, instead of making you look it up -- we put it in our response, and it starts on page 26. The closest that they come, that anyone comes, is Witness M, and what Witness M testifies is that there was a reserve police unit. Police are not members of the armed forces. In fact, article 43 of Protocol 1 specifically requires that, before police or paramilitary units are entitled to combatant status, so that they can become prisoners of war, a party that is going to incorporate their police into the military, has to inform the other party. There is no evidence of that here. There is no evidence that the inmates in the Celebici camp were in any way, shape, form or fashion members of a resistance group, or a military unit that was part of one of the parties. There does not have to be any direct agreement or written agreement saying that the Government in exile of The Netherlands recognises this partisan unit, this resistance unit in the occupied Netherlands, but there has to be some evidence that there is at least a tacit understanding, some kind of understanding, that the partisans belong to a party to the conflict. That is totally missing here. It is totally missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why were they detained -- not all Serbs in Bosnia were detained. Why were they picked up for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think the evidence from Witness D was, at a minimum, they were suspected of violating Bosnian national law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because they were linked with the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Linked with the other side, I do not know that is the test any place. It surely is not for prisoners of war. Just because there is a war going on, that does not give me the right to get my trusty shotgun and go off and become a combatant, absent being in a levee en masse. I have to be a part of a party to the conflict. In fact, in Pictet's commentaries to article 4 of the Geneva Conventions, Pictet discusses the history of article 4 and shows that the authors of the Convention chose to require this affiliation with a party before vesting prisoner of war status in people. I think the reason they did that was because, to give this special status of prisoner of war to people, they wanted to ensure that they were part of the armed forces of a party to the conflict. If you read article 4 as a whole, partisans and resistance people are part of the armed forces of their party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you interpret their evidence, is it not part of the argument of those detaining them that they were a risk to the security of the war effort?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I think that is real clear from Witness D's testimony. Given the fact that they were nationals of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Pictet's commentaries and the Geneva Convention on Civilians makes it pretty clear -- again, absolutely clear, that under international law the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina clearly have during international armed conflict -- I am presuming for a moment this is international armed conflict, I am not conceding it -- have the right to do pretty much what they want to do with their own people so long as they do not commit genocide or crimes against humanity. The best example I can give is out of my country. It is not one of the prouder moments of the US Supreme Court, but the Japanese internment cases from World War II. My Supreme Court held in 1943 and 1944, in cases which I cited in my pre-trial brief, or pre-trial memo, that it was perfectly legal for the United States to lock up Japanese-Americans, citizens of the US of Japanese ancestry, solely based on their ancestry. Again, that is not one of the prouder moments of my court and I would sure hate to defend that, but that seems to be the law. So, if the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina reasonably determined that these people were Bosnian -- if they were determined Bosnian nationals and they in fact were Bosnian nationals they would have a right to incarcerate and even if they were not Bosnian nationals, if there is a reasonable belief that they were a threat to the security of the State, then, at least under what Pictet says, article 147 of the Civilian Convention says, they have great latitude in incarcerating them, based on a reasonable basis that they constitute a threat to the State. Have I answered your question to your satisfaction, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If not, that is what I am here for, is to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are not disputed questions. You are merely making suggestions which you think, in your opinion, was why this situation had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is your view about it and you are entitled to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, absent a showing by the Prosecution of two things -- they have failed to make a prima facie case as to the Article 2 counts. The first is that there was an international armed conflict. Mr Ackerman talked to that, and I am sure the Prosecutor will talk to it and Mr Ackerman may talk to it again. The second is that the Prosecution must show that the complainant in count 1, the complainant in count 2, was a protected person under one of the four Geneva Conventions. That is, I believe, paragraph 15 of their indictment, which is incorporated in every remaining count. Absent a showing proof that they were not nationals of Bosnia Herzegovina, the Prosecutor has failed to show that they were protected persons under the Geneva Convention on Civilians. Absent a showing that they were prisoners of war under the Geneva Convention on Prisoners of War, that they meet that test that I talked about in article 4 of the Convention, they have failed to show that those inmates were protected under the Geneva Convention on Prisoners of War. So, in that case, they have failed to make a prima facie case as to each individual complainant. Levee en masse -- the Prosecution mentioned levee en masse in passing and said they may have constituted a levee en masse. Levee en masse, according to the Geneva Conventions on PoWs, is people that rise spontaneously on the approach of an invader; conceptually, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot invade the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It just does not work that way. The US cannot invade the US. The United Kingdom cannot invade the United Kingdom, even though my Irish ancestors may say they have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Even if there are internal dissensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there is an internal dissension you now have an internal armed conflict, and it is not covered by article 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So this is another stroke you are trying to pull. If you say the US cannot invade part of the US -- they can do so, to dislodge persons who are declaring themselves different -- and do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In the mid 1860s we had an event some of us call "the late unpleasantness", our civil war. Those of us who are from the southern States, or our ancestors, may have called President Lincoln's forces "the invader", but I do not think President Lincoln would have bought that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It depends on what side of the divide you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In a similar situation in your country, in the late 1960s, early 1970s, there was the Biafran rebellion. I suspect that the Government did not consider itself to be an invader of the breakaway areas. I think that as a matter of international law, it was not. What your country was doing and what the United States troops in 1861 were doing was putting down a rebellion, but there was no question about the boundaries of the United States ever changing. In the mind of the United States and really in the mind of the international community -- the international community, the United Nations, recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent country with certain borders. I think most countries in the world, by May 1992, had done it. Clearly the European Community did, the Security Council did, the General Assembly did. Bosnia cannot invade itself -- it just cannot do it. Command responsibility: that is an area which is a fairly complicated area of the law, and a fairly important -- very important area of the law in this case, both in general and as applied to my client. I would first like to talk about command responsibility in general terms, and then I am going to narrow it down to how it applies to Mr Delic. On our initial brief it starts on page 69. That is where the discussion starts. But, first, I would like to point to something in the Prosecutor's brief. One of the areas that we talked about was causation being a requirement that must be shown. That was, I believe, on pages 75 and 76 of our initial brief. The Prosecutor said on page 48 of his reply that we cited that with no authority and that is frankly incorrect. We did cite authority for the proposition that causation is an element of command responsibility and that authority was Professor Bassiouni's book, "Crimes against Humanity". It is cited in our initial brief and it is cited again in our response. Command responsibility started as a concept in international law with the 1907 Hague Conventions, and it came to its fruition, as applied to at least the military, with the post-World War II Tribunals. A couple of national cases and several cases that were tried by International Tribunals, or courts under Control Council 10 law in the occupied Germany. Control Council 10 set up the zonal courts so in the American zone the American judges would try cases, in the Russian zone the Soviet judges would do it and the French and British zones. Those key cases, of course, are the Yamashita case, the Toyoda case, the Tokyo Tribunal, and then the hostages case and the high command case. Looking at those as a group, with the exception of the Tokyo Tribunal, they all involved military commanders, and essentially there were four things that had to be proved -- four to five, depending on how you believe it, and we will talk about that in a second, on what you think the elements of the offence are. The first was the status of the commander as a commander. The second was that his subordinates had committed a violation of the law of war. The third was a knowledge requirement on the part of the commander about those crimes and we will discuss the knowledge requirement separately in a second. The fourth was that the commander either failed to take steps to prevent the crime, or failed to investigate and punish the perpetrators of the crime. That has been memorialised, if you would, in article 7(3) of the statute. That is a very separate concept from article 7(1) of the statute, which is a personal responsibility. Under 7(1), I am guilty of what I did -- if I planned a crime, if I ordered a crime, if I took part in a crime, I am guilty. Under a command responsibility theory, I am guilty because somebody else committed a crime and I did not stop it -- if I meet those criteria. The two unusual cases were out of the Tokyo Tribunal. One was the conviction of some members of the Cabinet of the Japanese Government for failing to -- or for allowing abuses against prisoners of war. The second was against General Muto, who was General Yamashita's chief of staff and I will discuss Muto in a minute, separately. Subsequent to the World War II cases, there was a lot written about command responsibility, but this is the first international court to try a case on a command responsibility theory, and apply international law, that I know of, since the post-World War II cases. After World War II, 1979, 1977, the Protocol 1 was adopted, specifically articles 86 and 87. Instead of using the word "commander" it used the word "superior". I believe, and I will show the court why in a moment, that what that was was an attempt by the parties to Protocol 1 to make it clear that civilians who were in control could be held responsible on a command responsibility theory. An example of that would be the Kahan Report from Israel after the massacres of the Palestinians by the Phalangists. The Kahan commission looked at the responsibility of the Israeli Minister of Defence, and found that, under a command responsibility theory, he was responsible for that massacre. I think the two areas of contention in general between the two parties here -- not speaking about Delic -- I will speak about Delic separately in a moment -- is the knowledge requirement and whether or not the defendants' acts or failure to account caused the crime. The statute says, "knew or should have known". In fact, that was the language that the United States wanted included in articles 86 and 87 of Protocol 1. The conference rejected that. I talk about that a bit in our response, and they used the standard which is different in the two official languages. The English official language says "possessed knowledge which should have enabled him to determine"; the French version is "possess knowledge enabling him to". There is a big difference. The three different standards are pretty -- are very large differences. Under the "knew or should have known" standard, which was rejected by the Protocol 1 Convention, if someone is not out looking for information, he could be guilty. Under the English version of Protocol 1, if he had information which should have enabled him to conclude that there was a crime committed, even if he never put all the information together or could not figure it out, he could be guilty of this offence. Under the French version, he has to have evidence that enabled him to conclude that -- enabling him to conclude. So, he would actually have to determine if there was a crime committed. I would submit that the proper standard is the French standard in Protocol 1. If Protocol 1 is -- if we are to consider Protocol 1 to be the law, international law on command responsibility. We should accept the version which is narrower, which narrows the criminalisation, if you would, because it is the general rule every place I have ever heard of. When you construe general laws you construe them -- fairly, but in such a way that you do not extend the criminalisation, but you narrow it -- you narrow what is a criminal act. Causation: when I sat down and read Professor Bassiouni's book I had not thought about causation as being an element of command responsibility, criminal liability. When I started to think about it, he is right, that no matter what I do as a commander or no matter what I do not do as a commander, if my acts or failures to act do not lend themselves to causing the crime, then why should I be held criminally liable for that crime, if my acts or omissions are not related to it? Professor Bassiouni notes that it may be a fairly difficult thing to prove, especially for commanders who are physically some distance away. In fact, applying a causation theory might, in my opinion, have caused a different result in the Yamashita case. But there has not been much that I have seen written on the requirement of causation. Frankly, with all the authorities I have read, and I have read everything I can lay my hands on command responsibility in the last year or year and a half, nobody has thought about causation, except Professor Bassiouni. For instance, a failure to punish this criminal offence may very well be the cause of the next one, or the failure to properly supervise subordinate commanders or subordinate units may be the cause of this crime. The failure to properly train one's troops in the laws and customs of war, as is required by the conventions may be the cause of this crime. Or, a refusal to investigate, or a cover-up may be the cause of the next crime. An example of that would be a case which I cited involving an American general, whose name suddenly escapes me, but cited in our brief, who was the commander of the division involved in the My Lai massacre in 1967. That was the case where a company of the US Americal division went into a village in Vietnam and murdered a lot of people, committed significant war crimes. The division commander did a cover-up investigation. There was no question about that. If his actions were not the cause of the My Lai massacre, his cover up of it could clearly be said to be the cause of the next atrocities committed by his division. Just because a person is a commander does not mean that he is guilty under a command responsibility theory, even if it is shown that his subordinates committed an offence. There has to be a showing, in my view, either of actual knowledge of a violation of the law, or that he possessed information leading him to conclude -- using the French standard, the French words out of article 86 -- that a violation of war had been committed, that he either did not take steps to prevent crimes, or he did not take steps within his authority to punish them, and that his dereliction was the cause of the crime. Hazim Delic: with the exception of General Muto, this is the first case that I know of where someone who was not a commander has been held responsible, or attempted to be held responsible, for criminal acts of others based on a command responsibility theory. The Muto court -- I cited a Law Review article talking that it was an aberration, of doubtful precedential value. I agree. It was on a different subject -- on the subject of holding civilian leaders responsible, but I think that, because it stands alone, the Tokyo Tribunal is a very, very doubtful precedential value. When you look at both the briefs that we filed, and the briefs that were filed by the Office of the Prosecutor, we cite case after case after case. I am just looking at their brief right now and I will just cite a couple. Toyoda, Admiral Toyoda was the commander at various times of the Japanese combined fleet, the Japanese escort fleet, and another subordinate command. He held those commands at the same time, and at the end of the war he was the chief of the naval general staff, so the man was either one of the highest ranking officers in the Japanese navy, or he was the highest ranking officer in the Japanese navy. He was tried as a commander -- command responsibility theory -- for the crimes that were committed by Japanese naval troops in Manila -- the same crimes that General Yamashita hanged for; same facts, same case.
