What the Prosecutor did not tell you was that General Toyoda was acquitted on all counts and the reason he was acquitted was because he did not have command of those troops -- even though he was superior in rank to every one of them -- each and every one of them. The next case the Prosecutor mentioned is the Mumathet case, and, reading their own quote, says he was an important figure in the concentration camp, "and, as an escort SS officer, wielded military power of command". They cite Supreme Court of the US, Yamashita, power to control the troops under his command. The Trial Chamber is aware that I am not fond of the Yamashita case. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is not a unanimous judgment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No. I think the part that everybody looks at is dicta -- it is just pure dicta, because the Supreme Court did not have to decide that issue. They were presented with a different issue, whether they had the jurisdiction to decide, and they said, "no, we do not". Let us talk about the rest of this anyhow. The medical trial -- Prosecutor's quote: "The law of war imposes a military officer in a position of command." Hostages case, the high command case -- I have cited, I have so many quotes on the high command case in our brief, I will not even get into it any more. It was commanders -- the people who were not commanders were held responsible for what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are based on strict tests with regard to the military command test.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You bet Judge, and here is why. They say I do not understand the theory of command responsibility. I do not know they understand what command is. Generals Divjak and Pasalic told you what command is. A commander, by virtue of the fact he is a commander and for no other reason, has the power of life and death over his troops. The personal power in combat. He can say, "Jones, you go out there and you take that hill. You are probably going to get killed doing it, but you do it"; if Jones does not do it, Jones goes to gaol. Only a commander has that kind of responsibility in the military -- personal responsibility. People who are not commanders may be delegated authority by their commander. The most influential person in any military unit I was ever in, after the commander, was the chief of staff. He was more influential than the deputy commander, he was more influential than anybody else, because he sat at the right-hand of the commander. When he spoke you heard the commander speaking. But that chief of staff has no independent authority, except over his secretary and his subordinates on the staff, and the high command case held that the chief of staff is not even responsible on a command responsibility theory, for crimes committed by his subordinates on the staff. It was the OQU -- everybody asked me what that is -- it is the operations officer, which again is a very influential position on any staff. Clearly, the customary law of war as applied to the military limits criminal liability on a command responsibility theory to commanders -- because they are commanders, because they are the people who have the personal authority under the law, under the regulations, and under international law. When you look at the authorities that have been cited for what military people believe, what nations believe constitutes command responsibility. I quoted Field Manual 2710 from the US army. That is because, frankly, I have dealt with it for years and I had a copy. The Prosecutors I think at one point quoted the British field manual. If they did not, Burnett's Law Review article I think it is talks about it, and says with the exception of a couple of words at the end it is the same. What does it say? Under some circumstances commanders may be held criminally liable. We quoted the Yugoslav regulations from the SFRY. What does it talk about? Commanders -- it does not talk about staff officers, it does not talk about deputy commanders -- it talks about commanders. Then we have Protocol 1. Protocol 1 does not use the word "commanders" in article 86, it uses the word "superiors". I would suggest to the Trial Chamber that the word "superior" rather than the word "commander" was used in article 86 for a real simple reason -- it was to get to the high ranking civilian -- the civilian official that has the power, the mayor who arranges, organises or allows atrocities. Frankly, let us get to Adolph Hitler, too. He was a civilian and not a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was a superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He was a commander in chief of the military, because he took that position, but he was a civilian. Spehr was a civilian. Many of those people were civilians, but they had what Fenrick calls "military command-like authority". They had the same kind of authority that a military commander has. That is what "superior" means in article 86. If military commanders or military people were to be tossed in with everybody else, why do you need article 87 that talks specifically about the duties of the military commander. It is the commander in the military who possesses this personal power. It is the commander in the military who has the duty under international law. It is the commander who is responsible for everything that his unit does or fails to do. What the Prosecution is asking this court to do is a couple of things. One is to abandon 50 years' worth of law now since high command and hostages and say that we are going to look not at the command, not whether or not he is a commander, but whether or not he has more stripes on his sleeve or whether or not he has more pips on his shoulders. Regardless of what you call him, someone who is not a commander lacks that kind of personal authority. Secondly, Commander Burnett, in his Law Review article which I cited at some length, talks about some policy arguments on why you should limit this to commanders. Remember that law of war, as we talk about law of wars, is to a great extent created by military people, for military people, and it has only been in the recent past that it has gotten outside of that. In combat or even in peace time a commander is the person who is responsible for that unit -- again, responsible for everything his unit does or fails to do. If it fails to do something, he is responsible. If it does something bad, he is responsible. If it does something good, he is responsible -- to his commander. If you start holding the non-commander liable on a command responsibility theory, what you are going to do is create an international law obligation for that subordinate to countermand the orders of his commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think the test that is laid down (inaudible) -- the superior is in a position to prevent or punish, but still he does not do that. He acquiesces in the end. That is the test to be applied. It does not matter what position he is in the military hierarchy. That is why they left off the chief of staffs in the high command case, they were not in a position to prevent or punish. This is the test they applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, General Divjak -- that is a good test to apply, because it is the commanders who have the power to punish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Or prevent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or prevent. The commander is the one who in his own name can do it and the commander -- the two Bosnian generals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Only in this position, he can prevent or punish.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is right. The Prosecutor tries to draw this distinction between a de facto commander and a de jure commander. I do not know what that means. Command is a legal status. It is frankly like being pregnant -- you are or you are not. You are either the commander or not the commander. If you are the commander you have these duties, you have these obligations, you have these powers to carry out those obligations. You may give some of this authority -- lend some of this authority to your subordinates, but you keep the responsibility, you can never delegate that responsibility, just authority. A de facto commander, whatever that is, because command is a legal status, he cannot have it. He may be some other kind of leader, but he is not a military commander. Even in a situation of a partisan unit -- the Prosecutor says you may not call them commanders. I do not care whether you call them George -- command is a function and it is a legal set of responsibilities, and a legal set of powers and even in a partisan situation, to be a military unit under article 4 of the Geneva Conventions on PoWs, they have to be part of the military of a party -- part of a party. When that party says, "Yes, that partisan unit out there is part of us, they are ours," they are vesting that commander with command authority -- the responsibility and the powers that go with that command. Otherwise, if that commander did not have that, then that partisan unit could not -- the members could not be entitled to prisoner of war status, because they do not have a commander who is responsible for his subordinates. It has to go to the commander. He has the power, he has the authority; he is, if you would, "the man". Are there any questions from the court on command responsibility, or have I covered that pretty well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there appears to have been a confusion between the superiors of the immediate commanders, who are deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where does the responsibility lie?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In any military unit, commanders command and their subordinates -- I am not talking just about the level of a five star general or field marshal. You get down to the squad level, there are 10 people -- nine people now, there are 9 people in the US infantry squad. One of them is the squad leader. For those purposes, he is the commander. The assistant squad leader is not. It is that squad leader, that platoon leader, and to a great extent it really does not depend on rank or experience. In the hostages case, the chief of staff had a much higher rank than subordinate commanders. He was a general officer. The subordinates were subordinates -- they were much lower ranking. The commanders of the battalions were probably lieutenant colonels. What it has to do with is the status of command, and when you say "superior", I believe that "superior" means a civilian with military command-like power -- the same kinds of power over subordinates as a commander. Because they have the power to order, they have the power to punish for failure to obey orders or for violations of the laws and customs of war. Very quickly, if the court -- have I cleared that up for you, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not quite. As between a brigade and a squadron, which of them, up to their higher authorities, if there are breaches within each of these hierarchies, where does the responsibility lie?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Justice Murphy in the Yamashita case, in one of the footnotes, asked the question you are -- answered the question you are asking. He said, "with this decision we may be sealing the fate of some future President of the US, and his chief military advisers". What you look at is the level of knowledge and control. An example would be the My Lai massacre. Telford Taylor -- General Taylor was the chief American prosecutor at the Nuremberg trials after the big trial. In 1967, 1968 and 1969 he wrote letters to the New York Times saying that President Johnston should be tried on a command responsibility theory for Mei Li. In fact, he is wrong. First, there is no showing anything that President Johnson knew -- that he knew anything about it. Hopefully, the President of the US has other things to do than worry about what a company of about 120 soldiers is doing in the middle of a major war. He has the whole war to worry about, plus running the domestic economy and everything else. In the normal course of business it would not get to the White House.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why did it get to that extent in the Yamashita case? Why was he responsible for what was happening in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was a military Governor and he should have known. The atrocities were so widespread. One of the dissenting opinions from one of the judges there thought that the evidence was not properly considered and the trial had been held in a hurry, and there were so many things which had to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I can tell you -- Yamashita kind of bears a special case in what some of the scholars look at. I can tell you how the US army Judge Advocate Court analyse Yamashita. They analyse it as abandoning his command. It was so widespread, there is no way he could not have known. He effectively abandoned his command, therefore he was responsible for what his command did because he abandoned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I want to find out -- is a sergeant. (Inaudible). INTERPRETER: Microphone, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It depends on the army. In my army you have two grades of private -- it has to do with pay rates. The private 1 makes a little bit less than a private 2 and then you have a private first-class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let us have private 2; is a private under him who is about to commit a crime, and he does not stop, is he not responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, unless he is in command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because of his said inaction --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It depends on whether or not he was in command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I do not think you go by the status of the person. The test is whether he is in a position to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And he does not stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In your hypothetical situation, Private E2 Jones may very well be the commander -- if the war has been going badly, very badly, he may be the highest ranking person there, and, therefore, under the general law of command, he would assume command of whatever unit it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So long as he is superior, the status does not count. And he is in a position to stop or punish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In a military situation that goes with command. The two are linked. Only the commander can punish -- General Divjak told you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Strictly speaking it is one of imputed knowledge, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You can have imputed knowledge. The high command case talked about that. They said that if there is a report in your headquarters, and it shows that there were crimes committed, the commander cannot say, "Well, I did not read the report, sorry." Those reports exist so the commander can know what is going on. If he is not happy with the reports he is getting, he can demand more reports. If he thinks people are lying to him he can send people out to check. That is why he has an inspector general. Yes, you can have imputed knowledge or you can have knowledge where you could not miss it. That is the Yamashita case -- it was so widespread that the court found General Yamashita had to know what was going on. On the other hand, the more famous trial out of the Mei Li case, involving Captain Medina, that was tried on command responsibility theory by US court martial. The trial judge said that there had to be actual knowledge, and in fact the evidence showed that Captain Medina, when he learned of the killings, when he learned of the murders, put an end to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Tried to cover up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The cover-up went a lot higher than Captain Medina. So, yes, you have to look at the standard you are applying. The article 86 standard -- article 86 has two standards, depending on whether you like French or English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We go by our own Statute, should we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But applying the Statute -- again because the Statute does not create substantive crimes -- and the Secretary-General made that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Rwanda Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, in the report for this Statute, he says we are not creating any crimes. I do not think that anyone at the United Nations would say that the Security Council is a legislative body that can impose substantive offences on governments. All that the Security Council did was take some provisions of international law and say, "We are setting up a court to try violations of these international laws." Judge, I just -- I may be found wrong on that by the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where do you derive the substantive law?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think the substantive law comes either from the Conventions -- clearly Article 2 -- you have to apply the Geneva Conventions. There is no way you can get around it, that is what Article 2 says, and you look at what those -- where there is a Convention, you look at the words on the Convention and you apply that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They define offences as such?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, article 144 of the GCC, and I suddenly have a mental block on which article it is in the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They name the offences themselves but they have not defined them as a court would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is clear -- you are correct, that nobody expected the Geneva Conventions to be the penal code. When our legislatures -- whether we call them legislatures, parliaments or congresses -- sit down to write penal statutes, they will do it in considerably more detail than is laid out in the grave breaches provisions of the Conventions. I think there is no question about that. On the other hand, some of these have pretty clear meanings under international law -- people know what they are talking about. Others are not as clear as they could be. I think we pointed some of those out in our brief. I am not real sure what constitutes various offences. There, you can run into a nullum crimen sine lege problem and a notice problem, that I should be able to know when I do an act or when I have an omission, whether or not I am subjecting myself to criminal responsibility. If I cannot do that, the Statute is so vague. I think that it is lunchtime. Can I have a few minutes after lunch and then I will sit down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will have to break in five minutes time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We can break now if the court would like. I can come back after lunch and finish in about 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will come back at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. During the break I went down and had a cold drink and saw us on the television and figured out that I did an awful job of explaining something. I would like to continue on that. It is this: it was really some questions that Judge Jan asked that I think I need to explain my position a little bit clearer. Rank and authority in a military unit can be two completely different things. It is fairly well known, for instance, that, in the Soviet army, commanders might have a lower rank than some of their staff officers. It was just the way they did things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The same in the civilian world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In the civilian world, that could be the same thing. Just because I have a higher rank than someone does not mean I have the authority to issue legally binding orders to them. From my army, because it is one I am familiar with, the chief of chaplains is a two-star general. He cannot issue an order to anyone except another chaplain. He has the rank, but he lacks the authority to use that rank. So, what you have to look at when you are determining superior authority, in my submission, is the authority to give a binding order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Control the action of the subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is right, to issue an order that binds him, on your own authority, and to punish him if he disobeys that order. Clearly, in the example that you gave, Judge Jan, Private E2 Jones can stop Private E1, because he has had a gun and can point it at him and can say, "do not do that". But that does not give him the legal authority to do that, to command or control the lower ranking private. That comes with a position. For instance, as with Celebici, there has been testimony here that a man named Zaho Mustavic was the commander of the guard, that he was in command of the guard force. I do not know where he is or what he is doing, but he is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is not before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He was the man, the supervisor, if you would, the commander of the guard force. He could order them, issue legally binding orders to them and, within the scope of his competence, punish them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where did you find that evidence, or are you merely assuming?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was the commander of the guard -- there has been testimony to that. There has clearly been testimony to that. As a commander, he would have the authority to issue legally binding orders. That is what commanders have. One author talks about it this way: he says the person committing the offence was under the command of the accused, that is, the accused had the authority to issue orders, not to commit illegal acts, and the authority to see that the offenders were punished. I think that is clearly what "superior" means in article 86 and in Article 7(3) of our Statute. If you lack the authority to issue legally binding orders on your own -- on your own authority -- and the power to punish for violation of those orders, then you are not a superior. Simply because you have more stripes on your sleeve or things on your shoulder does not necessarily give you that authority -- the legal authority. Again, the lowest ranking private, presumably, can prevent the highest ranking general from committing a war crime simply by pointing a gun at him and saying, "if you do it Sir, I will" -- but that is not what we talk about when we say the ability to prevent. It has to be the ability on your own initiative to give that legally binding order, and your ability on your own to punish a violation of that order. I hope -- have I made that clear, your Honour, on what my view is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think that is the correct position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And absent the authority to give that legally binding order, or absent the authority to punish a violation of that legally binding order, then you are not a superior for the purposes of article 87 and Article 7(3). So you have to look not at the rank, but at the kinds of powers that are given to this person. That is what the high command case did, that is what the hostages case did, that is what Toyoda did, and they found that, because -- they found because Toyoda was not in command at all, not anywhere in the command, he was not guilty and they found the various staff officers in the high command and hostages case were not guilty, because they lacked that authority -- to issue, on their own, those legally binding orders and to punish violations of those orders. One last thing, and I will sit down and I am sure the court will be happy for that, but the illegal detention count. The Prosecution has to prove two things on the illegal detention count. They have to prove protected status under the Geneva Convention for Civilians -- Convention IV, so you look to article 4 of the Geneva Convention for Civilians and see if these people fit that definition. If they do not, if they are not in the hands of a party of which they are not nationals, they do not fit the definition. Even if they do fit the definition, then the detention has to be an illegal detention. So, both things have to be shown. Pictet, in his commentaries to the Geneva Conventions, notes that States have broad authority to detain enemy aliens during time of war, and that they have traditionally been given this broad authority. There has been evidence from Witness D about the fact that these people were, at a minimum, suspected of crimes. We pointed out in our joint brief that it is not at all unusual in criminal justice systems to have pre-trial detention. The best example I can think of is in American law -- and it is laid out in our brief -- under certain kinds of cases, there is a presumption that the person should be detained pre-trial and, secondly, there is a presumption, and a very strong presumption in this Tribunal, that there should be pre-trial detention. In fact, as I understand the holdings, a person will be detained pre-trial absent exceptional circumstances, so there is a clear presumption of pre-trial detention. Given that, and given the circumstances of the arrests of the people that were detained in the Celebici prison, I do not see how anyone could say that there is at least not some suspicion that they constituted a danger to the State, and under those standards, clearly the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the right to detain them. Your Honours, unless there are some further questions, I think I will sit down and I think Ms Residovic is next to talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If those are the only submissions you want to make, that is okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. My colleagues, Mr Ackerman and Mr Moran, have presented the most relevant points of our joint request, so, your Honours, I am going to limit myself to the part that speaks to the general superior responsibility and, as regards Mr Zejnil Delalic, with individual counts and I will show that the Prosecution has not shown the prima facie case and that this indictment needs to be rejected on all counts. Allow me, your Honours, just to remind you very succinctly of what we have submitted in portion G of our request, that my client, Mr Zejnil Delalic, was accused of superior responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3), points 13, 14, 35 -- 34, 44, 45 and 7.1 -- under Article 7.1, for his personal responsibility and that is count 48. In count 3 Mr Zejnil Delalic was identified as the coordinator of the Bosnian and Croatian forces in the Konjic area between April and September 1992, and as commander of the Tactical Group 1 from some time in July until November 1992, and in point 7 of the indictment, his superior responsibility was based on his control over the Celebici camp, and that he was in a position of superior authority with respect to all the guards and all the units who entered the camp. So, these provisions reflect charges on all counts, and the Prosecution had the burden of presenting evidence, which would lead to the conclusion that my client had such responsibility, or, as spelt out in the Statute, that there was a prima facie case for each count under which the accused has been indicted. Mr Osberg has very specifically stated that the Prosecution evidence will show that Zejnil Delalic took part in the work of the War Presidency of Konjic; that he took part in the work of the War Presidency; that he played an active role in the attacks on Bradina and other villages in the Konjic area; that in these activities he was the person of superior authority over the Celebici prison and all staff who worked there; that this was a direct position of superiority; that he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were committing crimes and that he did not prevent these crimes, nor did he punish their perpetrators. The Prosecution also had the burden of proof to establish the direct or indirect command responsibility, whether it is jure or de facto, and especially emphasise that all personnel who were linked to the prison were connected to Delalic and were related to him -- to his authority in that period of time. The Prosecution further claim that they would establish the chain of command that goes from the guards to the deputy commander and camp commander and then on to Delalic himself. The position of the Prosecution towards my client has been made unclear by the fact that they would not discuss the authority that Zejnil Delalic had on paper, and that, by assuming that there was no specific body which would be a superior body over the Celebici camp, that it was my client's, Zejnil Delalic, who actually acted in this role, so in the first phase of the presentation of her evidence, the Prosecutor herself was not clear about what function my client discharged at that time. They said that it was some time in April, but the presentation of evidence shifts this to the second part of May 1992. Also, the Prosecution is not clear on whether my client discharges this duty and has this responsibility also as a commander of TG1, but the Prosecution has committed to proving all these facts. From the first moment the issue of Zejnil Delalic's authority as a superior person was linked to the general questions of superior responsibility. The Defence has submitted from the beginning that Zejnil Delalic did not have a role of superior authority in the Konjic area in this period of time in which he has been charged. We have started from the general criteria and standards set out in the Tadic case and we believe that, in this case, the facts are such that not only has the Prosecution not established a prima facie case, but, furthermore, the Prosecution has shown that Zejnil Delalic did not have superior authority over the Celebici camp and its staff and, therefore, we say that all charges against him relating to this charge need to be dropped. In this stage of laying out the standards for our request to dismiss the charges, which we have set out in our written brief, we also point to the fact that this Tribunal in other cases also clearly pointed to the Prosecution as having the burden of proof, and that if they are not able to establish a prima facie case through their presentation of their evidence, the indictment against my client needs to be dismissed. We are basing this on all the evidence that was presented and accepted by the Trial Chamber in this case. We say that every element of the case that is set out in the indictment needs to be proved and I need to show what these elements are. I will try not to repeat myself, and I will try not to repeat the submissions that have been provided in the written brief, but I will comment on what the Prosecution has provided us in their reply. My colleague, Mr Moran, has given our arguments about the general superior responsibility, so, in order for the Article 7(3) to be implemented, that is, the 7(3) Article of our Statute, we first need to determine what the status of this person is. In other words, we need to decide what is the prima facie -- that is what are the grounds for suspicion that this person in this particular case, Mr Zejnil Delalic, had a role of superior authority. Why is this necessary? This is necessary because, absent prima facie, the status of the superior authority cannot be determined and, therefore, needs to be dismissed. The Defence of Zejnil Delalic has submitted that Zejnil Delalic was never a commander or coordinator of TG1 -- was never in a position, that is, never had a status of a superior authority, both with regards to the Celebici prison, or the staff of the Celebici prison, or persons who entered the Celebici prison, and committed the acts set out in the indictment. Even though there is a discrepancy in time between the opening statement of the Prosecution and the evidence that was later submitted, I think that the facts will speak for themselves. The Prosecution has first submitted that, in this first period, that is, as coordinator, our client, Mr Delalic, had an implicitly military position and that his responsibility flows out of that position of authority which he held. This makes the situation for the Defence, and we say that the Prosecution cannot determine the prima facie case against our client on this basis, so all the evidence that has -- that was presented by the Prosecution has corroborated our position. At no time was a chain of command established, that is, between the guards and the soldiers who entered the prison and committed these crimes, and the absence of these proofs should be sufficient grounds for dismissal of charges against him. Because we say there is no prima facie case against my client, maybe that should be the end of our argument of this Article 7(3). He cannot be answerable for the acts of third persons of which he did not know, and we can also -- we also cannot talk about his responsibility for something he did not know anything about. In this connection, in our written submission, we followed a certain order. In its response, the Prosecution has also followed that order, saying from the beginning of May Zejnil Delalic had the status of commander. Your Honours, we have heard a large number of witnesses. Very few witnesses spoke about Zejnil Delalic. That very fact places Zejnil Delalic in a different position from the others in this case. Unfortunately, the proposal of the Defence to separate the trial in order to establish whether Zejnil Delalic had the status which would correspond to a status of an accused person was not accepted, and we were forced, in this trial, for two years now, to expect the evidence to be presented which would possibly speak of Zejnil Delalic as someone with superior authority over the prison and the persons entering the prison. What Zejnil Delalic did and what was he in this period in Konjic -- I think the answers to these questions can best show whether he was a superior and whether the Prosecutor has, through the evidence presented, established a prima facie case to show his superior position. In our written brief, we covered the period from 18 May, when Zejnil Delalic was first appointed by the coordinator, between the War Presidency and the Defence forces of Konjic. The Prosecutor, in his response, claimed that Zejnil Delalic in this period had the authority of a superior and presents facts linked to the special appointment of 2 May, according to which Zejnil Delalic was appointed to take care of certain logistical affairs. The Prosecution also refers to TV Zagreb programmes in which the journalist introduces Zejnil Delalic as a commander. I can say straight away that that evidence itself speaks to the opposite. The evidence presented before this court, referring to the special authorisation dated 2 May 1992, was issued by a civilian body -- the War Presidency of the municipality of Konjic. This evidence was issued in the form of a special authorisation on the basis of a decision of the War Presidency on certain logistical affairs; therefore, a clearly civilian authority appoints a clearly civilian person to take care of clearly civilian tasks and duties, which the municipality, within the framework of its own obligations, in a situation of a threat of war, needs to carry out certain preparations and to provide logistic support for Defence. This evidence offered by the Prosecutor clearly shows that Zejnil Delalic had no military position or function. Another piece of evidence that the Prosecutor is offering in response to our request is the title given by the journalist and the way the journalist addresses Zejnil Delalic in May in Zagreb. I wish to refer you, your Honours, to other evidence which reveals what Zejnil Delalic said in this connection; "Surely you do not think that the journalist in Zagreb appointed me to a military post". A few days later Delalic was appointed coordinator of the War Presidency and we cannot see how a commander would, 10 days before -- who was called a commander 10 days earlier, before being appointed a civilian authority. Therefore, there is no doubt, your Honours, that the evidence, including the special authorisation for logistical affairs, as well as the way Zejnil Delalic was addressed by the journalist on TV Zagreb and the other evidence offered by the Prosecutor, such as the testimony of Generals Divjak and Pasalic and other persons who worked in Konjic at that time showed Delalic had absolutely no military function. General Pasalic said, "I had a coordinator because I appointed him to coordinate between the army and TO forces in Konjic. He had certain military authorisations, but he was my subordinate, therefore a coordinator is never a superior". If a coordinator is never a superior authority, then Zejnil Delalic could not have been one, either. That same witness said that if a civilian authority appointed the coordinator, then it must be a predominantly civilian function and he must be liable to the civilian body that appointed him. Therefore, from the documents on the appointment, it is clear that Zejnil Delalic in this period did not have, nor was he appointed to any kind of military function, and the task that he had as a coordinator, that is, to coordinate between the War Presidency and the Defence forces, to this post he was appointed by a civilian body, which could have transferred only the authority that it has itself, which means not the authority to issue commands or to have control. Therefore, in this period, Zejnil Delalic did not have any authority of a superior person of any kind and especially not as a military superior authority. According to the allegations of the Defence as described in our written brief, the period in which Zejnil Delalic carried out coordination was the period from 18 May until the earliest, 27 July, which means that, after 27 July, that function is no longer performed, because a dispute occurred with the HVO and when Zejnil Delalic went far away from Konjic and, therefore, was a whole month participating in combat operations. The only evidence we can rely on for this period is certainly the testimony of the generals that we heard here, and who said clearly that a coordinator is not a superior function. This also confirms the position of the main staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which said that this function had no relation to the command functions in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that conforms with the statement of Zejnil Delalic, who clearly described his tasks as a coordinator. This evidence which we are presenting to the court, and the witnesses that we heard, and who were examined and cross-examined -- all those witnesses confirmed this thesis of the Defence. Therefore, the Prosecutor has not confirmed through any evidence at all that, in this period, Zejnil Delalic had a military or a civilian function, which would have any superior authority with which he could have issued orders, supervised the execution of those orders, and punished those who failed to carry them out. The evidence presented before this court clearly shows that the additional order, for instance, for the battles on Bradina, were signed by the HVO commander of the operations at the time in Bradina. We also saw that, at the time, in Konjic, there was a joint command between the TO and the HVO, as of 12 May, and this is a fact that can be verified through the videotape found and seized in Zdravko Mucic's apartment. It is clear in the period May and June, according to the evidence presented in this court, Zejnil Delalic engaged in logistics and various other activities to support the War Presidency in its activities. The actual appointment as a coordinator -- this document clearly shows, as I have already said, that he was appointed by a civilian body; that is, by the War Presidency. Furthermore, that appointment shows that the Presidency appointed him within the framework of the preparations or defensive preparations in the territory of Konjic municipality; therefore, in the framework of those tasks which, according to the law, belonged to the municipality -- a municipality which has absolutely no authority to issue, order, or to establish any military structures in that area. Your Honours, reviewing these documents, I wish to interrupt my presentation and to draw your attention to the fact that the translation of this appointment of Mr Zejnil Delalic is not correct, so I would like the translation service to correct it. I hope it is a translation error, because what has described as the task of the coordinator has been incorrectly translated. In point 2 of this decision it is stated that the coordinator of defensive forces will "directly coordinate work between the Defence forces of the municipality of Konjic and the War Presidency". Unfortunately, in the translation included in the record the word "between" has been omitted and that word "between" existed in the previous translation given to us by the Prosecutor, and prepared by this Tribunal. This word is not without significance, because the word "coordinator" means a relationship between two bodies and the word "in between" in my language, and I believe in yours, too, indicates this relationship "between", rather than any relationship of superiority. Therefore, it is visible from the tasks given to him by the civilian body to coordinate activities, to mediate under very difficult and specific conditions of life in Konjic, it is not possible to deduce from this definition any other conclusion but that Zejnil Delalic was a person carrying out orders by the superior body and not a superior himself. This is another argument of the Defence, that the Prosecutor has established the opposite, that is, that Zejnil Delalic was not a person of in superior authority. In the general allegations regarding the responsibility of the commander and of superior command, the question is raised: when can a civilian have a status of superior command? We have asserted that that can happen only when that civilian person has the same authority as a military commander. I would not repeat that part of our argument, but it is clear from what I have said about a coordinator that this was not a civilian function, nor a superior civilian function and still less could he have any authority that could be compared to the authority of a military commander to issue orders, to control, or to punish perpetrators. In any event, the Prosecutor has not offered any evidence to show that Zejnil Delalic, as a coordinator, had any person as a subordinate -- even a secretary. The Prosecutor, in its response to our motion, drew attention to some actual powers of Zejnil Delalic. As the evidence has shown, Zejnil Delalic was not a member of any political party, nor was he a member of any political body, nor did he have any kind of State or political function, and, in our written submissions, we have highlighted the statement of witness Sabine Manke, the witness Petko Grubac and drawn attention to all the things that have been clear from the beginning as stated by Zejnil Delalic. This evidence of the Prosecution has not corroborated the allegation that Zejnil Delalic had any State, political or other similar function which could give him the position of superior command in the sense discussed in the general introduction. The question that is raised is until when Zejnil Delalic was a coordinator. According to Zejnil Delalic's Defence -- and this has been corroborated through much of the evidence -- he performed the function of commander of Tactical Group after he was appointed on 27 July -- when, from the Vranjske Stijene, which is 40 kilometres east of Konjic, he moved to the area of the city of Sarajevo -- that is the area of Igman and Pazaric, which is more than 60 kilometres away from Konjic. Therefore he ceased to act as coordinator even before -- that is, on 27 June, when he joined the combat operations at Vranjske Stijene. That this is true has been confirmed by the evidence presented in court -- the Prosecution evidence. Their witnesses, Pasalic and Haraz, met with Zejnil Delalic as a coordinator in mid July at Vranjske Stijene. Dokto Pel told us when he was released from prison, Zejnil Delalic had just arrived from Glavaticevo, which is a locality right next to Vranjske Stijene. Also, all these facts are confirmed by Exhibit 126/1. The Prosecutor, in her response, claims that Zejnil Delalic had a significant role in the military operations conducted around Konjic. Contrary to that, this Trial Chamber has admitted as relevant and authentic evidence Exhibit 124, that is, the order to the TO commander of Konjic, issued by the Supreme Command and signed by Sefer Halilovic, whereby this municipal staff of Territorial Defence is instructed to start military operations in the direction of Boracko Jezero, Nevesinje and Kalinovok. Furthermore, another exhibit has been admitted. That is the coordination of war operations in the municipality of Konjic, D125/1, from which it is clear that the commander of this operation was the commander of the TO staff, Esad Ramic. These exhibits confirm best that there is no question of a leading military role of Zejnil Delalic in this period. These are authentic exhibits that were presented and admitted by this Trial Chamber which speak to the contrary. A part of these activities which Zejnil Delalic, as the coordinator, and assistant to the War Presidency in establishing relationships with other entities, faced with formidable war tasks and what the situation was like in Konjic -- you have heard from various witnesses like Dzajic, Zebic and others, you have seen some of the videos, too. Therefore, throughout this period, the tasks of the coordinator were linked to securing a minimum of living conditions for the population, and for 25,000 refugees, who, within a short period of one month, reached Konjic, which was daily exposed to at least 60 shells. At the same time, he coordinates between the Defence forces of the Konjic municipality and the War Presidency, which was not able alone to establish that link with these forces and I am referring to the MUP, the HVO and TO, each of which had its own chain of command, some relating to Grude, another to Sarajevo, a third towards the Ministry of Interior in Sarajevo. Nowhere in the chain of command can Zejnil Delalic be found. This was a time, as General Pasalic said, when combat operations were being carried out, living problems being dealt with and at the same time army being established under conditions of war. In concluding this segment relating to the functions of the coordinator, as a predominantly military post, or rather a civilian person with military authority, it can be said that, viewing the evidence in the most favourable light for the Prosecutor, the only thing that can be said is that Zejnil Delalic, carrying out his functions appointed -- given to him by the War Presidency, were the functions of a coordinator and all the other evidence shows that he did not have the position of superior authority. The Prosecutor, in her response to our written request, is trying to refer to certain exceptional circumstances under which a person can become something like a superior authority, but not in a legal sense but, rather, in a de facto sense. On the other hand, we have the evidence presented in court, and the testimony of a number of witnesses that speak to the contrary. There is the testimony of Generals Divjak and Pasalic, who clearly stated in Bosnia-Herzegovina, immediately after the outbreak of war, a decree was passed on the organisation of the army, that 15 April is considered the day of the founding of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that in Konjic, already, on 17 April, a new staff was constituted in line with the new regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that a member of the Republic staff visited Konjic to assist that army in organising itself, and to adjust its activities with those of the HVO. Furthermore, General Divjak not only confirmed that provisional instructions were issued on the organisation of TO staffs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but General Divjak was the author of those instructions and, as Professor Gow would have said, if they testified differently, because they are more familiar with the situation, one should rely on their testimony. This witness, your Honours, clearly showed that the municipal staffs were subordinated to district staffs in accordance with these instructions, such as was the case in the area of Mostar and the municipal staffs were directly responsible to the staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, in no chain of command -- military chain of command can we find the coordinator, that is, Zejnil Delalic. As I have already asserted, his role was absolutely a civilian role. The next argument that is offered by the Prosecutor is trying to prove that Zejnil Delalic did have the authority to issue orders and refers to an order establishing a railway connection between Jablanica and Pazaric. Among the same evidence there is another argument and another exhibit that has much greater weight. That is Exhibit 116, which clearly shows that, on the day the railway line was opened, Zejnil Delalic said that he was carrying out orders. What Zejnil Delalic said on Konjic television in June was interpreted in an identical fashion by General Divjak, who said that a coordinator cannot sign orders, that he may have signed it because of his lack of experience regarding orders, or as somebody executing an order, or as a witness of the issuing of such an order. The Prosecutor is trying once again to establish the superior authority of Zejnil Delalic and his link to the prison through the fact that Zejnil Delalic signed three discharge papers for prisoners. In our written motion, we have devoted sufficient attention to this point. According to the testimony of Witness C and other witnesses that we have heard, who were actually released, it is clear that several hundred people were released from the Celebici prison. Only three discharge documents, which at the moment we saw them, your Honour Judge Jan, you saw that they were not identical to the other ones. There was a signature there, which witness Miro Golbuvic read out as being the signature of Zejnil Delalic; but that signature was on behalf of someone else. Therefore, it was on behalf of the head of the investigative commission and in all situations, and especially as indicated by the witness Petko Grubac, this means that the person who signed those three discharge documents had the authority to do that, given to him by a third person. What is, however, much more important, Zejnil Delalic has been accused as the coordinator and commander of the Tactical Group. Not a single of those discharge documents was signed by the coordinator, or by the commander of the Tactical Group. Any third person may, upon permission of another person, sign such a document, so that Zejnil Delalic could not have done this in his function as a superior authority. As for any kind of link between Zejnil Delalic and the Celebici barracks or prison, from which the Prosecutor would like indirectly to adduce that Zejnil Delalic was a person in superior command, is illustrated by the fact that he entered the barracks perhaps once, twice, three times, that he spoke to Witness D, and that he signed these three discharge papers. Let me just remind you of the testimony of witness Belin, who said that the barracks covers 85,000 square metres consisting of many buildings, and you saw dozens of truck on the video. You also saw, on the basis of the testimony of witness Belin, that the prison covered less than 5 per cent of the whole compound area. Anyone who enters the Celebici prison need not have any superior authority. The fact that he entered the compound does not prove anything. To view this in the most favourable light for the Prosecutor, the testimony of Witness D can be reduced to a couple of elements only. Probably, he met Zejnil twice -- when Zejnil was explaining what he should do on one occasion and a second time what the commission should do. A command and superior responsibility does not imply explaining things to anyone. It implies issuing orders, control and punishment for lack of observation of orders. Therefore, this crown witness of the Prosecution, apart from saying that he received a uniform, which is normal for a logistics man to do, except for confirming that the Croats were appointed by Croats, except for saying that he came upon instructions of Mostar HVO to Konjic, that he went to the HVO to recount certain events that he saw in Celebici, the fact that he said that he never saw the original of the document that was offered here as a report on the situation in Celebici, that he said that he never informed Zejnil Delalic of the situation in Celebici -- he said nothing more than that. This testimony has absolutely no effect on the judgment of this court, whether the Prosecution has proven the position of Zejnil Delalic as a person with superior authority. Regarding the arguments we have presented regarding Tactical Group 1, my comments will be very brief. I wanted to show that the coordinator had absolutely no military function and particularly not any key military function, as the Prosecutor is alleging; that he had no superior authority, and still less a military superior authority, and that Zejnil Delalic in this period had no relationship with the prison or prisoners and the Prosecution has not offered any evidence which would place him within the chain of command going from the guards up to him. Just one more sentence: the civilian body that appointed him, according to the constitution and the law, has no authority regarding the formation of prisons, or the appointment of commanders to prisons and, therefore, that body could never have given him any such authorisation. As for the position of Zejnil Delalic as a person in superior command in relation to the prison and the personnel in it, while he was commander of the Tactical Group after 27 July, I think that the testimony of General Divjak and General Pasalic was so convincing; these generals were shown a large number of documents, and orders issued by Zejnil Delalic as commander of the Tactical Group, the commander of a Tactical Group which has a temporary and provisional war task, and the task of that group was to try and lift the blockade of the city of Sarajevo as the worst and most serious war problem for all the defensive forces in the country and that it did not include any responsibility that could be compared with the responsibility of district staffs, or the responsibilities of cause. Therefore, he had no authority over the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We were talking about municipal staff and the district staff. How do the two differ? Nobody has explained that, but I was wondering, where does the district come and where do the municipal staff come?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, a city with the surrounding villages constitutes a municipality. Several municipalities constitute a region, several regions constitute a district. This is how the Territorial Defence organised before the war and this structure, as explained by General Divjak and as presented in the provisional instructions offered as --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am getting Serbo-Croatian in my English -- I am not getting an interpretation. I hope we can have some help here so we can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Someone in the interpretation booth might give us a guide. Are you tuning to number 4?

utterances.text: I am on number 4, but I am hearing Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I have clarified this point, so a city is subordinated to a district and General Divjak testified that three cities were not under the Republican staff -- that is Mostar, Gorazde and Banja Luka. So Capljina, Konjic and others were linked directly to the Republican staff in Sarajevo until the Army Corps were formed. I hope that this clarifies the issue. In this situation, the Prosecution would want us to forget the testimonies of the two generals and that the appointment of all forces, that is, that this would also include the authority over the Celebici prison and the staff that worked there. However, I believe that you still remember vividly the testimony of General Divjak, who said that all forces does not mean all forces, because that is impossible. That does not exist in law. Such function does not exist in law. There must be certain combat forces and certain means, certain materiel that are also assigned to a commander. We presented several pieces of evidence from this wider regional area, where these tactical groups were active, and you could see the tape of Prozor -- the TG commander, Sabic, who, when this area came under control of the HVO, that he reported it to Zenica, which means a completely different region, different area, from where Zejnil was. Zejnil was assigned to the forces that were going towards Sarajevo and all other forces were under the command of the Zenica staff. Professor Gow testified to the same thing. The Hadzic area was in the area of activity of Zejnil and General Divjak explained that certain forces from that area were subordinated to him at that time. However, as Professor Gow stated, all these forces, before the war and at the beginning of the war, were subordinated to the Sarajevo staff and then, as it developed, to the BiH Army -- to the Corps I. It could have been strange to hear General Divjak say that all forces is not all forces, but General Divjak did, very lucidly, explain this point and it was further corroborated by the exhibits that were submitted. So, the Tactical Group has a provisional, temporary and limited task, and within that scope, it can receive specific tasks from its command -- tasks which it is supposed to carry out, and it has to have specific forces which are subordinated to it, and in the testimonies of the generals, such a view has been admitted, and it shows that Zejnil Delalic did not have superior authority over the Celebici camp during that period. I want to remind the Trial Chamber that Zejnil Delalic replaced Colonel Polutak in this duty. It is not possible that certain of the functions just follow the person of Zejnil Delalic and not the functions which he discharged. So if he was a coordinator, somebody else was a coordinator, so if there was a commander after him, the responsibility would fall on him afterwards. I just want to point out that the Prosecution has offered no evidence that Zejnil Delalic was at any point the person of superior authority over the Celebici prison. We have shown that the generals have explained the two orders that Zejnil Delalic wrote on 24 and 28 August, which could link Zejnil Delalic with the Celebici camp. However, they clearly stated that these were orders in which he was a transmission of the main staff, because, in the preamble of these orders, it is clearly stated that he is carrying out the orders of the general staff, and the points relating to the Celebici camp speak about a need to conclude the investigation at the Celebici camp and that is a commission which is not part of the Celebici camp, and Witness D testified that this investigation commission was outside the institution of the prison and it was a body formed jointly by the HVO and the TO, so even this transmission was not directed towards the camp and the activities in the camp but to one specific task. This task was to speed up the work on the investigation of the detained persons so that the law could apply to all of them. In the Prosecution's response, I went back to the arguments submitted in our written brief and through all it, it can be demonstrated that there is no prima facie case of Zejnil Delalic's superior authority. On the contrary, it all points to the fact that he did not have the status of a superior authority. I am also going to point out another objection raised by the Prosecution in their response to our brief. The Prosecution is surprised that in a written brief we have not at all commented on the Vienna documents. Allow me, your Honours -- so far I have talked about the authenticated evidence presented to us, which clearly showed that Zejnil Delalic never had a position of authority, especially not a superior authority, over the Celebici prison. At the moment when he became the commander of the Tactical Group, he was obviously a military commander, and he had a position of superiority over his subordinates. However, the Prosecution offered no evidence that the soldiers subordinated to Mr Delalic ever entered the camp and committed crimes. Had they done so, Mr Delalic would be responsible pursuant to Article 7(3), but since the Prosecution offered no evidence in that respect, I felt that I had no need to respond to that. To the question by the Prosecution why we treated the Vienna documents in this particular way, that is, ignoring them, I am going to answer by the following. The formal reason is that the night before last we received the answer to our submission -- to our appeal. While the matter is pending, we could not act on this matter, but the real reason is that, after so many -- so much evidence has been introduced, and some of which were confirmed by the custodian of the archive of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I say that this evidence, by comparison -- I will not say they have no value whatsoever, because this is not the time to bring this point, but they cannot change the fact that the other evidence has actually proven a different matter. Why do I say this? Most of the documents found in Vienna were not authenticated. We do not know who provided them. We do not know how they are related to the indictment. We do not know the context. We do not know who the authors are, and in what context of time they wrote this. If this was -- we cannot -- if we do not know the author, we cannot bring a witness who is going to refute anything, and our position in that respect would be very difficult. We do not know what the context was in which the author wrote this document. Was this a joke? Was this because he was in a particular mental state? Was this because he was inebriated? Was this because in one of these documents it says, "We were forced to lie", so maybe the author had to lie for some reason, or maybe it was an anti-propaganda to counter the terrible propaganda that was waged against Zejnil Delalic at the time. So, these are not authenticated documents and cannot be made to be a prima facie case about any function or position of Zejnil Delalic and, even more so, given that other evidence points to the opposite. But, since this evidence was accepted by the Trial Chamber, and given the standards of authenticity, I am just going to give you several examples to demonstrate why it is justified that we ignore these documents and we say that they cannot determine the prima facie case with respect to the status of Zejnil Delalic. Most of these documents contradict themselves. In Exhibit 124, it says that, "because of the tensions over there, we were forced to lie". So, that points to the way in which these documents were drafted. In Exhibit 118, which allegedly was recognised by Zejnil Delalic, which appoints him to the post of commander of Tactical Group 1 -- and this is part of the first group of exhibits -- it is not an issue whether Zejnil Delalic was appointed the commander of the TG1 and that he replaced Mustafa Polutak. It is also clear when this happened and also Zejnil Delalic recognised the document which bears the date of 23 July on its fax headline, but recall witness Haraz, how these things were communicated. Zejnil Delalic said, "I found this appointment in August when I arrived at Igman", so the document is not controversial in itself, but it does not corroborate any charge against Zejnil Delalic. Then Exhibits 137 and 141, which were introduced through witness General Pasalic, also further corroborated this evidence which I have just quoted. The 137 from 7 December is a letter of the Corps IV -- Pasalic to Halilovic -- and it talks about the arrest. It does not talk about Celebici, about Serbian prisoners or any crimes committed against Serbian prisoners, so in December -- as late as December, General Pasalic has no knowledge about any crimes committed there. Had he had any, he would have reported it. Then, Exhibit 141, about the desertion from the army, and others also are pertinent in this respect, because they do not speak about the Celebici prison or the Serbian detainees there. Both documents must be viewed within the context of the testimony of General Pasalic, because, for instance, there are some functions mentioned there about Edib Saric and, when asked, this witness said, and this is very important, that he did not check the functions, nor the persons mentioned there, and that he relied on the report of his commission. You have evidence on the function of Edib Saric as part of the evidence admitted. Relying extensively on the Vienna documents, the Prosecutor clearly shows that she does not have real evidence to establish a prima facie case against Zejnil Delalic, and he then -- she then provides interpretations, such as, for instance, "He played an important role in the Donje Selo operation, and one can see from the video he is ordering an attack on Donje Selo". Please view that tape again. You will hear many voices. Zejnil is nowhere. You will not hear his voice and there is no expert for voices -- perhaps the Prosecutor had an expert -- to judge the voices that can be heard on this tape. Subsequent exhibits have to do with the image on image programme -- the salute on the occasion of Gajreta, and Esad Dramic is mentioned on a number of occasions. Your Honours, let me recall, there are two witnesses who can say with authority who was the commander -- Omer Boric, TO commander in May, and Esad Dramic, TO commander as of 1 June. The first witness was on the Prosecutor's list, and the Prosecutor did not call him -- in answer to my question whether the witness did not wish to come, the Prosecutor said, "No, we are abandoning our plan to hear this witness". Another witness who could have spoken about all these things was in front of the door under a subpoena. The Prosecutor did not bring him in. All of us here present have a lot of experience -- many years of experience behind us, but an assessment of evidence is an ability that we all have. When a Prosecutor does not bring in his own witness, it is because the witness cannot confirm what the Prosecutor wants. Actually, that is the obligation of the Prosecution under Article 68 -- under Rule 68, to disclose exculpatory evidence. The Prosecutor did not do this and is relying on unauthenticated pieces of paper, which would refer to that witness. It is true the Prosecutor did carry out part of its obligation under Rule 68, informing us that Esad Dramic had said that Zejnil Delalic was not his superior. If we take all this into consideration, your Honours, rounding up my argument in response to the Prosecutor's response, I can say that all the evidence presented by the Prosecutor in the past year has confirmed one thing: Zejnil Delalic, as a coordinator, nor as a commander of Tactical Group 1, was not a superior authority over the prison, or its staff. He was not responsible for the work of the prison, for the work of its guards, or for the activities of persons entering the prison. Zejnil Delalic does not have the status of a superior authority, either as a civilian in his capacity as coordinator, nor as the commander of a Tactical Group, as he was on combat positions far from the town of Konjic. For these reasons, all the counts of the indictment relating to Zejnil Delalic should already, at this stage, be dismissed, because no prima facie case has been established, which in our language means that the Prosecutor has not established reasonable grounds, on the basis of which an objective observer, seeing all this evidence, could conclude that Zejnil Delalic was responsible for any of the charges that are made against him. Your Honours, let me very briefly comment on some other elements of Article 7(3). Zejnil Delalic, as a person; did he know, or have reason to know, that something was happening in Celebici, or did he prevent or punish, or investigate and punish the perpetrators? This portion will take a short period. I do not know whether we should take a break now, or should we break at 4.30? I do not know. Advise me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think if you still want to continue, we can go on. We might break at 4.30 for the day, because we want to join the plenary, so we will continue tomorrow morning. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Only if it is determined that somebody has a position of superiority, that is, that the perpetrators are subordinates to the superior person -- only then the elements of responsibility have been established in pursuant to Article 7(3). As I said, all evidence points to the fact that Zejnil Delalic did not have the position of authority, but, since these are legal points for which prima facie needs to be established individually, if there is no evidence that he knew about this, the charges should be dismissed. If there is no reason why he should have known that it also should be dismissed, and if the person had no real possibility to punish the perpetrators, that is also prima facie and the charges need to be dismissed. These are the legal grounds and I only want to make several comments on each of these particular issues. My learned colleague, Mr Moran, talked about some theoretical aspects of this superior authority. However, in order for knowledge to exist, it has to be real knowledge. It has to be a fact -- the fact that he was present there, that somebody told him of it, that he received information that clearly states that his subordinate has committed a certain crime. However, the Prosecution has offered no evidence of this kind, that he knew that they were committed or that they were about to be committed. In our written brief, we have tried to give a detailed submission of this position of ours, and we have stated that there has been no evidence shown that Zejnil Delalic not only was present at the time when these crimes were committed, but also that he was not in the area when these crimes were committed. There was an incident about the accidental firing of a gun. Four witnesses have testified to it. Two of these witnesses know Zejnil Delalic and his family personally. Two of them said that he was there alone, and one said that he recognised Amir Delalic and the other two said that the "boss" or the "chief" would come -- do not know Zejnil Delalic in person and what they stated before in this Trial Chamber is hearsay and is not indicia, let alone evidence. Because, additionally, it has been established that Zejnil Delalic was not there, because one witness who knew him, Milvan Kuljanin, confirmed that it was not Zejnil but Amir Delalic who was there. If we add to that that two additional witnesses did not know Zejnil Delalic and that Dr Grubac pointed to an uncanny similarity among the Delalic brothers and some cousins, and even put some people who knew them from sight could not distinguish between them, that adds weight to our contention that he was not there. Witness D testified about many things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, you appear to be going to the evidence in detail. I do not think that is a matter for legal argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you, your Honours. We gave detailed submissions in our legal brief on that, but I am just pointing out that there are numerous points showing that he did not know -- he could not know about any crimes. Professor Bassiouni points to a number of elements that need to be established in order to prove that a commander could have known what was happening. All evidence presented before this Trial Chamber and which are in our written brief, pages 35 through 38, clearly point out that Mr Delalic could not have known that certain crimes as described in the indictment were being committed in the Celebici prison. We pointed out all the problems relating to the area where Zejnil was over those two months and the fact that no clear evidence has been presented that he had the relevant knowledge. As far as the arguments relating to measures to prevent such acts, I completely second everything that my colleague, Mr Moran has pointed out. I would just like to add that, witness Pasalic and other witnesses clearly stated that in Konjic at that time there were no law enforcement forces, and there was no judicial system. That is the position, the person of superior authority, even if they knew about certain acts, they had no way to implement any measures against it. It was only later in the year that these things were established in Konjic, and a number of cases were conducted after that, but the person who was supposed to punish and to prevent these acts from being committed was not present in Konjic. In Mostar, they were there throughout this time, in Sarajevo later in the year and in Zenica in the fall, and then, due to the conflict with the HVO, this area was blocked and no persons could have been prosecuted there. Again, the Prosecution offered no evidence that the Republican bodies changed the rules of the authority; that is, that they had given Konjic the authority of prosecution, so that even if there was a person of authority who knew that there was a person who needed to be punished, they lacked the means of doing so at that time. Just one more comment on that issue. My colleague, Mr Moran, pointed out that punishing -- measures to punish something would also mean preventing these acts from occurring in the future. Zejnil Delalic started discharging the function of superior authority in August and we see that these acts subsided by August, and we see that, even following the ICRC visit in August, there are no more acts of this kind. I am not saying who is the person who was supposed to prosecute. I know that I was in that position for 17 years, and so I know, but I know that, in this case, no prima facie case was established and this is a condition sine qua non of establishing responsibility of my client, so no point of Article 7(3) has been established and all the charges relating to that need to be dismissed. I am only going to take five more minutes and this is relating to the personal responsibility of my client in persecution of civilians. My client did not imprison or detain or decide on the detention of civilians, and my colleague, Mr Moran, said that, as confirmed by the witness, these were persons who were, in a period of immediate threat of war and a state of war, had blocked the area. He said that the responsibility of the commander is to de-block and to arrest everyone. They had arms bought on the black market or obtained through the SDS and possession of weapons is against the law. Therefore, if they were detained, this detention could have been lawful. This, of course, does not justify the commission of any bad acts against them, but this was not unlawful detention. It is, rather, the conduct of proceedings against those persons, some of whom testified that they had been tried. As with respect to this charge, count 48 of the indictment, there is no evidence offered by the Prosecution to establish a prima facie case, or, rather, for an objective observer, if he were to analyse all this evidence, he would come to the clear conclusion that Zejnil Delalic is innocent and that the indictment against him should be dismissed on all counts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your contribution. As I indicated just recently, we would like to rise now and continue at 10am tomorrow morning, instead of continuing now and having a break within the next 10 or 20 minutes. The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 4.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, 12th March 1998, at 10 a.m.
